utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Call the case, please, Mr. Court deputy.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-01-48-T, the Prosecutor versus Sefer Halilovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Good morning, ladies and gentlemen. Today we'll spend some time continuing our discussions on the statements of Mr. Halilovic. On the 24th March 2005, the Defence filed its written submissions indicating that it would object to the use and admission of the exhibit the Prosecution will seek to introduce through the witness Mr. Okic. This document is a statement of Mr. Halilovic dated 8th November 1993, and it was given in the course of the Trebevic operation. On the 30th of March, 2005, we had some discussions on that issue, and the Prosecution stated that Defence has merely made allegations, most of which, according to the Prosecutor, are hearsay. So we decided to hear the parties on this issue, and the Bench has some questions to the parties. I believe that the first question is addressed to the Defence. Why has the Defence not filed this motion any sooner considering that the statement has been part of the Prosecution's exhibit list since 7th June 2002.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, it wasn't appropriate to canvas the matter before the matter was assigned to the Trial Chamber so we had to wait until that time. Frankly, I can indicate that it was simply a timing question for us and a matter of preparation. We came to this witness in the form that we did. Obviously we'd prepared to some degree to cross-examine in the future, but the reason for the lateness of it is simply that that's -- that's when we arrived at it and that's when we had time to consider the matter. It was simply a time pressure issue in respect of that. Your Honours, if I could indicate -- I'm not sure to what extent it helps but I came into this case -- I first came here in September of last year, and look, there's a history to it. I'll explain it if it helps the Court, but in broad brush that's why, because having weighed up all the matters, I as lead counsel took a decision to challenge it reasonably late. I don't deny and in fact I make it quite clear that at all times I had in mind that it was likely that there'd be a challenge to it, but I just wasn't able to turn my mind to it in the relevant way. I had to rely very heavily on -- I would make that very clear too, Mr. Mettraux, in drafting that document and dealing with it. So that's the answer as to why it was done at the time that it was. The other reason I'd advance about it is, perhaps mistakenly, I hope not mistakenly, I understood that normally speaking that the objections were taken at the time when these documents are to be introduced into evidence, and really it was as out of an abundance of ever caution to do it before Easter because we realised that it contained some substantive law, and my learned friend Mr. Mettraux obviously put a considerable amount of work into it. We thought that -- that's why we delivered it before Easter rather than on the day, simply objecting when the witness stood up to give that evidence. But yes, that's the reason why it was done at the time it was, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: In your submissions, you made several allegations, if I could use this term, that interview used the techniques which were forms of coercion and psychological pressure. The interview lasted up to 17 hours a day. Mr. Halilovic was not given access to lawyers at any time during his interview. Mr. Halilovic was not cautioned of his right to remain silent. Mr. Halilovic was not informed of his right to have counsel present during the interview. Mr. Halilovic was not warned that the statement he made may be used in evidence. And there are implicit threat of violence during the interview. Can you be more specific on that issue?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, yes, I can be. It depends how Your Honour wants me to proceed in respect of that. Obviously we have instructions from Mr. Halilovic that he's told us what happened, but I'm not a witness in the case, and I'm not sure whether it's appropriate for me to say what I'm told about that beyond what -- beyond what's in the motion there. And that's I think one of the questions that's going to arise here, do you need to hear evidence about these limited questions, and quite frankly in the common law system, you would need to hear evidence about it. It's not good enough for the barrister simply to make the allegation. If the Prosecution takes issue with the facts that are alleged, then the question arises how are they proved and they have to be proved in a normal way. That's the fact. But I can certainly way what the basis of the implicit threat is. The implicit threat is that Mr. Ugljen came along and said to Mr. Halilovic, "we can deal with this whole question another way," meaning that you can answer the -- which was taken to mean, well, you can answer these questions as they're asked or we can think of some other way of dealing with the matter. The context of that other way and that was specifically articulated to -- to Mr. Halilovic, is that he'd been arrested or been -- been taken into custody and asked to be questioned concerning Ramiz Delalic, Celo, and Musan Topalovic, Caco, and it was made quite clear to Mr. Halilovic that Caco had by some unfortunate means been killed despite surrendering himself into custody. So that was the context in which that comment was made, and that comment about Caco meeting an untimely death was made to Mr. Halilovic on a number of occasions, and we say that's the basis upon which Mr. Halilovic had a well-founded idea that it was a better idea to answer questions than to keep silent. So that's what that is based upon, and, yes, so that's the answer to that part of Your Honour's question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. And there are some questions that I would like to address to the Prosecution. Before that, would I like to remind the Prosecution of the Celebici case, that is, the Prosecution has to show that the statement of Mr. Halilovic was given voluntarily, there is no oppressive conduct in obtaining the statement. If the statement was given without the presence of counsel, whether the accused has voluntarily and expressly agreed to proceed without counsel present. So, Mr. Re, I believe that you have made your submission last time, but we would like to know some more details on this aspect. I wonder whether you would tell us if Mr. Halilovic was given access to the counsel or was informed of his right of remaining silent before taking the interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I thank Your Honour for the opportunity to address you, to address the Trial Chamber on this aspect. We are, of course, aware of the Celebici case, that the Prosecution must prove that the statement was voluntarily made. There are, of course, as the Trial Chamber appreciates, two people present in the building at the moment who would be able to shed light on the question the Trial Chamber has asked, that is the accused himself, Mr. Halilovic, and Mr. -- Mr. Okic. As Mr. Morrissey rightly points out, he isn't a witness. He wasn't there. He doesn't know what happened. The Defence submissions are full in the Prosecution's submission of assertions which are not supported by any evidence and my learned friend's submission as few moments ago in relation to Mr. Halilovic's treatment, or alleged treatment, at the time of the interview is, again, an assertion which is not supported by any evidence before this Court or even at the very least an affidavit from his client or anything from his client pointing to the circumstances of the detention. The Prosecution can rely only upon what Mr. Okic himself has told us in the statement and in the proofing notes which we have provided. Now, the Prosecution, we say, if we did not have Mr. Okic to give that evidence, we would not be relying -- we would not be relying upon this document. We would not be trying to put it into evidence. And it is only because we have the person here, one of the only two people in the building who can tell us exactly what happened, here to give that evidence that we are prepared to submit that we say after hearing the evidence of the witness as to the entirety of the circumstances surrounding the taking of the statement. At that point we would submit that it should be tendered into -- into evidence. The difficulty we have at the moment is that we have something on paper. I have conferred with the witness. The witness has confirmed his statement to the Prosecution. But in relation to this witness, we make a further submission, and that is that the witness himself, Mr. Okic, as I informed the Trial Chamber the other day, wanted to speak to the Defence. Now, the reason for that was he thought he was a Defence witness when he came here, and he thought that he'd actually made an agreement with the Defence to be their witness and to come and give evidence for them and he said he signed an agreement with the Defence to be a Defence witness, and we're in this very strange situation on Monday and I was saying, well, this is the first I've heard of it. We haven't heard anything of it, but we'll speak to the Defence and you can speak to him -- speak to the Defence and see what the situation is. Now, that of itself does suggest something in terms of whether the Defence were going to use him as a witness or not, and their view Mr. Okic as a witness of truth. We're only referring to one witness, one statement at the moment. The Prosecution accepts that Mr. Halilovic was interviewed over a number of days. Now, we don't have -- we don't have evidence on that. We don't have evidence as to the circumstances of his arrest, if in fact he was arrested, whether he was detained, whether he was at home, how he was treated on the other occasions. We don't know anything about that. There's only one person here who does. That's Mr. Halilovic. The evidence we intend to call relates to the interview on the 8th of November, and the witness will say that on that occasion, there are a number of interviews and on that particular occasion Mr. Halilovic did not request a lawyer and a lawyer wasn't present, but this particular interview continued in the same way as all the other ones did, and it's a continuum, but we're concerned with only one of those interviews. So in relation if Your Honour's specific question as to this particular interview, that's something we would have to ask of the witness. The witness will say, I anticipate, he didn't ask for a lawyer and we didn't talk to him about a lawyer on that occasion because he'd been in there. We'd interviewed him on a number of -- I had interviewed him before. I think the first date was on the 31st of August. That was Mr. Okic. I think this was the -- it should say it in the proofing notes, the first -- the first paragraph. Yes. This was actually the second interview. It's in the third paragraph. The 31st of October and the -- the 8th of November. So Mr. Okic will say on that occasion, I anticipate, Mr. Halilovic didn't -- didn't request a lawyer. Now, there is no law. Mr. Mettraux of course in his submissions, detailed submission, has quoted from the International Convention on Civil and Political Rights, the American Convention on Human Rights, and the European Convention, and quoted from the I think it was Article 14(3)(G) of the ICCPR, which is of course the right against self-incrimination. There's nothing in the ICCPR guaranteeing someone the right to a lawyer while being questioned by authorities. There is a right, an absolute privilege against self-incrimination, which of course is -- which of course is enshrined in the statute here. But waiver of the right to a lawyer or having a lawyer there is a different concept altogether. Now, Mr. Okic is the person who can tell us whether or not Mr. Halilovic waived his right to a lawyer in that particular interview, which is where it comes down to the question of whether you decide the interview was voluntarily or whether there was an element of coercion. The Trial Chamber -- in our submission, you can't decide this upon the Defence hearsay assertions, or assertions from the bar table as to how long he was interviewed for and the circumstances. In the Prosecution's submission, some of the -- some of the submissions the Defence has made, and Your Honour read out some of them along the lines of Mr. Halilovic was not given access to a lawyer at any stage during the interview, well, there's no evidence of that. That is -- this is an assertion. It's not footnote -- it's not footnoted because there's no -- there's nothing they can footnote it to. They could footnote it to Mr. Halilovic, and Mr. Halilovic could of course give evidence on this point only for the purposes of determining the admissibility of the record of interview and nothing further. The Defence alleged psychological pressure. They said, paragraph 26, "one form of Prosecution witness has indicated that coercive methods were used during Halilovic's interview," and they're referring to -- and I don't know how you'd properly describe it, but the addendum, if you could describe it that way, to Mr. Popovic's statement which apparently is something Mr. Popovic added later when speaking to Defence investigators in a very -- in a most ambiguous manner it appears to the Prosecution where he refers to "Psychological pressure." Now, I took the liberty of course as I had to in speaking to Mr. Okic who was there with Mr. Popovic if that were correct. It's in the proofing notes. He says -- and he's here to give the evidence that no psychological pressure was applied. But again that's hearsay in the sense that it's not a signed statement. It's a -- it's an assertion contained in a document. It's not a signed edition. It's not an affidavit from Mr. Popovic. It's basically a letter from the lawyer saying he said that to us. It's in a very different category to sworn evidence or a signed statement if Your Honours were considering, considering that, using that as part of your determination. In my respectful submission, the Defence should have brought a signed statement or an affidavit from Mr. Popovic outlining exactly what they mean by psychological pressure. Mr. Okic will of course say that of course everyone was tired at the end of -- at the end of an interview, as everyone is tired at the end of a day in court, and of course everyone is stressed, and of course someone who is being questioned would be -- would be stressed. But the Prosecution takes great issue with the assertions made in the submissions by the Defence in which they say that they -- it's basically one step of saying what Mr. Halilovic signed was beaten out of him. It almost -- it almost goes so far as to that. They refer to coercive methods not quite amounting to torture but pretty much getting there. Now, they're pretty serious allegations to make, and if you're going to make allegations like that you have to bring some proper evidence of it even if it were in the form of an affidavit from their client as to the circumstances of his arrest. We just don't know. So the Prosecution says -- our submission is that the only way that this can be properly determined is from hearing on this very point from the witness who was actually there, Mr. Okic, who in his dealings with the Prosecution hasn't wavered from his view or his professional view and at the time he'd been in the service since 1979. So he was no novice. He was no rookie. He had been there 14 years by the time he took this particular statement, and he's well qualified to talk about the normal methods that were used in interrogating people, the laws under which Mr. Halilovic was interviewed, Mr. Halilovic's demeanour during the interview, whether he was in military uniform, whether he was armed. Mr. Okic will say that he did have his weapon with him. How he came there. He was brought in every day by a military police officer, escorted from, Mr. Okic thinks, Supreme Command Headquarters and an interview conducted, according to Mr. Okic, in a civilised correct, polite manner. The only person we understand who can tell us that is Mr. Okic, and the Prosecution urges upon the Trial Chamber to hear from Mr. Okic about the circumstances of the taking of the statement and then make the determination as to the admissibility. And that's what I said the other day about the evidentiary onus shifting, because then it becomes a matter of admissibility. If the Trial Chamber determines that it was voluntarily made, it makes it prima facie admissible, the Defence then would have to persuade the Trial Chamber that it should not be admitted, if the Trial Chamber doesn't decide to exclude it under Rule 95 where is where the challenge is being made, but decides it would then turn to the exclusion under 89(D) if you reach the test of 89(C). Does that assist?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Let me give you some very initial response from the bench. I believe that this Trial Chamber is governed by the Statute of the Tribunal and the international standards of human rights. It is not bound by any national rules of evidence. As a rule, any evidence obtained by means contrary to international protected human rights is to be excluded according to our Rules, the Rule 95 of the Rules of Procedure. The second issue is that it is not the question whether the accused waived his right to have a counsel. It is a question whether the authority offered him or informed him about his right to have a counsel present at any interviews. That's two different matters. Thirdly, we noticed that the statement of the accused is called additional or supplementary statements, so I believe that is the part of the statement. Maybe often the first page of the statement on the first day of the interview the authority of Mr. Okic says something about the accused's rights. So I wonder whether there's any transcript, tape record, videotapes available so that to have us to understand that matter. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Well, I fully agree with what Your Honour says there. The Prosecutor gave you a 20-minute answer but the answer to your original question was no, they don't have any evidence that Mr. Halilovic was offered a lawyer, and that seems to be the end of the case. If the Prosecution has got such a transcript or such evidence that he was offered a lawyer, then of course they should be entitled to put that evidence before you. We'd like to see it. So if the Prosecutor says that that's the case, let them say so now and then they may proceed. At the moment, they're calling Mr. Okic, who wasn't there at the first interview. And Your Honours will be aware he -- when my learned friend says there are two people in the building, there is another one they should have called and that was Himzo Popovic. Now, Mr. Popovic was an officer who is the witness they should be calling and they're too scared to in my submission. He was there in the first interview and he was there with an officer named Borisa Delic, and he could say presumably if they call him what happened in the first -- remember that they've got the onus here, of course. So if they wanted to prove what happened at the start and that everything was done properly and Mr. Halilovic wasn't threatened and nobody came and mentioned Caco and Caco's demise and all that sort of thing, then of course they could call one of the officers who was present at that. Actually, they've taken that witness off their list. So, Your Honour, the current situation is this, that the Prosecutor concedes that they've got no evidence of offering a lawyer to Mr. Halilovic. And when Your Honour asked that question, that was one of the questions I was going to ask in cross-examination if we ever got to that point. It's clear one. But the Prosecutor may have an answer we may not know about so perhaps I better stop and let him answer that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Morrissey, before you sit down there's a question to you from the Bench.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: We allowed Mr. Okic to meet the Defence because the parties agreed on that particular matter, which to me it would be very strange.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Would you please give us some explanations on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I will, Your Honour. I'm very happy to. Obviously I found it strange as well, and I mentioned it to the Court because of that. I met with him -- Mr. Re of the Prosecutor sent us an email indicating this desire of Mr. Okic to speak to the Defence, so I then -- we then sought to make contact during the day. We couldn't do that. I think from recollection we mentioned it to the Tribunal before we actually spoke to him. I just can't recall now, but I think we did. And then in one of the breaks we spoke to him in a room just there. Now, Mr. Okic apparently was an English speaker. I went there with legal assistant Mr. Cengic and also an intern, both of them who were Bosnian speakers, but as it happened Mr. Okic was able to communicate with us in English and we spoke to him. We asked him what it was he had to say to us. We asked also for the Victim and Witnesses Unit person to remain in the room with us, but she said that her procedures were against that. So in terms of what happened in there, we didn't have a tape recorder with us at the time, of course, but so far as the discussion there, I would not have seen any witness alone myself, so that Mr. Cengic and our other legal assistant were present at that time or an intern, actually, were present at that time. Now, the discussion took place. He indicated to us that he had in the past spoken to two Defence investigators a long time ago. Those two are still both Defence investigators. Ms. Delalic is present in court now; she was one of them, and Mr. Dzambasovic, who Your Honours have seen on many occasions here, is the other one to whom he spoke. Because I had the possibility of cross-examining him, I didn't want to ask him any questions because -- depending on whether it was going to be a hostile cross-examination or not we don't know. So I really wasn't concerned to press him greatly. I asked him for some details of what he did and for some details of his impressions. He indicated that he had in the past spoken to those people, that he had expected to hear from them again and that he hadn't heard from them again since that time. Now, I can go into the details of what I asked him if that would help the Court. I'm -- we're not concerned by it, but they were essentially questions about what -- what was his recollection about particular aspects of the interview. One was whether it was a military security interview or whether it was being conducted by the state security officers. He gave us an answer. I don't know whether Your Honour wants me to tell you what he told us at that time. I'm happy to if it would help. I must say I -- the whole procedure's highly irregular, and I -- you know, as counsel I -- I make it clear to the Court, frankly, that I don't like this proofing that goes on. I'm not comfortable with it. In my system you don't do that. But it may be other systems allow it. The Prosecutors here do it. It leaves counsel open to allegations if a witness says later on look I never did say that to Ms. Chana, you know, this is all being made up. I only said I saw six bodies and Ms. Chana told the Court he saw ten bodies in proofing; that creates a problem. Almost I don't like those things very much and that's -- I must say it was a short conversation. Now I ask the Court, do you want me to tell you what -- what was the questions and answers I had with that witness because I'm very happy to say if that assists. So it's a matter for you, Your Honour. I'm very happy to say it as far as I remember it. I'm sorry, my learned friend Mr. Mettraux also indicates to us that -- that he provided to us at some stage a signed statement concerning his involvement as he remembers it in these matters. So -- and I -- and as is apparent from other witness, there is number of witnesses spoken to by the Defence counsel, most of whom who say they weren't offered 50.000 Deutschmarks or had their family threatened. Your Honours, many witnesses were spoken to by Defence investigators over time, many of them, and in many -- in respect of many of them we have statements, Your Honours, and this witness Okic was one such witness who was spoken to. Mr. Popovic is another such witness who we spoke to and in fact we've annexed, I believe, a signed copy of Mr. Popovic's statement provided to the Defence to the motion. Your Honours can only guess at the moment, but I suppose it's probable that's why they're not prepared to call Mr. Popovic because they know what's going to say and that's psychological pressure was brought to bear on Sefer Halilovic and Popovic was the senior person, was the person who was conducting the interviews and was there at the start, and was there throughout this month when he was interviewed. Now, Your Honours, that's -- those are specific matters to raise. I've got a few responses to make to my learned friend's lengthy answer but really that wasn't what Your Honours were asking him. You weren't -- as I took it, you were asking him a specific question about the lawyer in that situation, and his answer after all was said and done is they've got no evidence. They can't discharge their onus. The case is finished. If the matter is to go further, well, it can go further but Your Honours have posed the question whether there is something more. Your Honours will bear in mind, of course, that in our materials we've annexed -- we've annexed to that material some further material. The letter from the lawyer is one that's annexed to our motion. The statement of Mr. Popovic is also annexed. It should be pointed out, when my learned friend says that there's an ambiguous answer in there, there's nothing ambiguous about it. Popovic says that psychological pressure was brought to bear and that Mr. Mikhailov was not prepared to put that in the statement. But it should also be pointed out that in a subsequent statement taken by the OTP and in particular the investigator named Mr. Ken Corlett who came along after Mr. Mikhailov, presumably to clean up the mess, Your Honours, that statement makes it quite clear that to the OTP he also said that Sefer Halilovic was under "quite strong psychological pressure." And if the Prosecutor wants to draw your attention to that they can. But if they don't, I will. So, Your Honours, rather than respond substantively now, I just perhaps will stop for a moment because I've got some responses but at the moment they're not necessary because at the moment the Prosecutor's telling you that Halilovic wasn't offered a lawyer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Re, you want to take the floor?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yes, please. Prosecution takes issue with my learned friend's repeated attacks on Mr. Mikhailov. There's no open season on Mr. Mikhailov in this Trial Chamber. He's not entitled to take a shot every -- every day or so and talk about someone else coming in to take -- to clean up the mess. My learned friend just made some veiled allegations about the conduct of the Prosecutors here, the lawyers, in relation to not calling Mr. Popovic. My response to that is simply this: Your Honours will be appreciative there have been some changes in the Prosecution lawyers over time, and there were basically a new team came in at the end of last year, and two days ago I moved to put another interview on the list that I only found myself on Tuesday or Monday, I can't remember which one now, when I was preparing for this witness. Now, that says something about the state of preparation in relation to calling witnesses in relation to this particular interview, and yes, it did fall short, which explains why we didn't call Mr. Popovic when we were reviewing the witnesses we were to call in this case at the end of last year, at the time when the trial date was set, and we were reducing the number of witnesses from -- I think it was 107 down to 38 live witnesses. We looked at it and saw that there were two witness who is gave evidence of the same record of interview, and we chose one of them. We were not as cognisant as the Defence was of the significance of Mr. Popovic having been at the first interview. There is absolutely nothing sinister about our choosing Mr. Okic over Mr. Popovic, and had we known that there was going to be a challenge to the record of interview, the statement, which arrived, as Your Honour said, last Thursday afternoon, on Easter Thursday late in the afternoon, we would have called Mr. Popovic. We just didn't know. It is rightly a matter that should have been determined in limine before the trial began which would not have allowed us not even to open on these matters, the Trial Chamber having determined that matter. So that's our response as to why we have taken Mr. Popovic off the list. If it assisted the Trial Chamber, we could of course ask to put him back on the list. We have no fear of calling Mr. Popovic to get him to explain what he means by psychological pressure because we are only dealing with one interview and if at the end of the day there is a conflict between two witnesses as to what actually happened in an interview, well, then the Trial Chamber has to make a determination as to who to -- who to -- whose version to prefer. Of course there's always the option of the Court itself -- the Trial Chamber itself calling Mr. Popovic if you wish to hear from Mr. Popovic. That option is always open.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm very loath to interrupt and I apologise for doing so but I have to do it on this occasion. The Defence objected to Mr. Popovic being withdrawn from the witness list. Your Honours will recall at one time you were presented with a Prosecution application to withdraw witnesses, and you might remember that -- that application before you were very familiar with the case. But the Defence at that time objected to him, Popovic, being withdrawn. So in light of that I'm astounded by the submissions being made and perhaps my friend may better clarify it because we asked for him to be kept on. Anyway, I'm interrupting but that is an important matter. If my friend wants to raise that now, that better be clarified. That was done in January.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Well, had the Defence made it clear they were challenging the statement as they have as of last Thursday, we would have examined Mr. Popovic in another light. I've made that clear. Firstly, we accept that we weren't as prepared as we should have been in relation to this statement; and secondly, we weren't warned that there was a challenge to it. So that's as far as I can take it. The other -- the other thing is, Your Honours, in relation to the right to -- or in relation to whether Mr. Halilovic was advised of his right to counsel, the only evidence if you can call it that which is before the Trial Chamber at the moment is the letter in French and in Bosnian from Mr. Halilovic's family's lawyer, family lawyer, which suggests that he had a -- access to a lawyer. The Defence asserts that he was under house arrest and a lawyer made representations to higher authorities, the Presidency. Now, that certainly suggests that he had access to a lawyer at some point. As to transcripts of the -- of any of these interviews, the Prosecution doesn't have audios, transcripts or videos of the interviews. Mr. Okic will say, if he testifies, that he himself was unaware if that particular I view on the 8th of November was being taped or transcribed or videoed. If it was, he wasn't doing it. Although he said because of where they were it could easily have been taped and he wouldn't necessarily have known about it. The Defence in their own motion have said that they have tapes and transcripts. I don't know whether it's transcripts that they have. They have the tapes and some things are different to the statement. Well, one would expect that. A statement is always different to a taped transcript of a -- an interview is always different to a signed statement because statement is a summary. It's a composition as opposed to a narrative or a conversation between two people. They are -- they are of necessity different. The statement is always much, much shorter than a transcript of a conversation. If the Defence have it, I invite the Defence to produce to the Trial Chamber the tape where it says that Mr. Halilovic was in some way coerced or prevented from having access to a lawyer or didn't waive his right to a lawyer, because the Prosecution's submission in relation to this particular one, the 8th of November, is that at that point, he did not ask for a lawyer, and at least in that interview he waived his right to a lawyer. Although Mr. Halilovic, of course his family had a lawyer. Mr. Halilovic as an educated general in the army would, of course, have been completely aware of his right or of the fact that he could ask for a lawyer if he wanted to. But he hasn't asked for a lawyer -- we're talking about Bosnian law in 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: We have spent more than 40 minutes on this issue. We believe that in this situation the rule of the best evidence should prevail. Since we have a witness here outside, maybe the Bench could propose that we'll hear this witness only on the ways and the means to obtain those statement without going to the substance and the contents of that statement. And the Defence will have the full right to cross-examine that witness on any issues they made, so-called allegations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, could I just raise a couple of procedural matters about how that should -- how that should happen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, frankly, it's entirely proper for that to occur. The Prosecution are entitled to attempt to establish through this witness the relevant facts in a non-leading and proper way and I don't object to that being done. The only issue that I have is -- is to clarify the status of this evidence. The question is, is it admissible in the trial generally or is it just to be limited to this issue. And the reason I raise that is because my learned friend mentioned in an early stage of these discussions the possibility of conducting what he referred to as a voir dire. Now, Your Honours, a voir dire is a device that's used in common law situations. It's referred to in the Celebici case. In short terms, a voir dire in the common law system is a device that's used to shield from the jury certain controversial evidence that might be relevant to a particular point of admissibility. In the common law system, the jury is seen as somehow fragile and unable to sort out irrelevant prejudicial material, whereas Your Honours as professional judges can do that and can set aside such material. If you decide to exclude it, you can do so. But nevertheless the device could be useful here and I could understand my learned friend raising it as it did. It pay be it's an appropriate thing to do. But the question is, are we going to use that device with this witness and if the Prosecution chance to satisfy the onus, although at the moment it sounds as if they're not going to, but if they let us assume that something changes and that they do, then the question then arises as to whether other evidence ought to be called for and admitted on that point. It seems to me that it would have to be at least for Mr. Popovic in the current circumstances. Then the Tribunal will have to rule and perhaps create some brief rules about what is the status of this evidence. In the common law system, on a voir dire, the evidence admitted on a voir dire is not evidence on a trial itself. It's just evidence called to assist the court, the trial judge to determine whether or not to admit the evidence. Then once that decision is made that evidence is then set aside entirely. The exhibit or the evidence that's being challenged is admitted into evidence and then Defence must decide whether they want to cross-examine and if they do how to deal with it.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel please slow down for the benefit of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I'm being asked to slow down a little bit there. So that's the way that such evidence is dealt with in the common law system. Now, in this case, it may or may not be useful to do that with Mr. Okic but it probably is necessary to do it with the other evidence in the case. It is also possible in the common law system to admit the evidence from the voir dire later if the parties agree. In other words, if Your Honours make a ruling on material and you exclude the evidence or admit the evidence or say it can be used or can't be used, at a later time the parties might think, we don't need to go over all that again and we could agree to admit that evidence into the evidence as part of the trial. But it is a live issue; it always has to be dealt with in the common system, and it always has to be determined in advance. So I would invite the Court to make to -- to make a ruling about that before we start. My submission is that -- is that we should conduct this as a voir dire in the common law system, whereby the evidence is not admissible on the trial generally but it's relevant solely to the questions that are before the Court and that way it's completely confined. The only cross-examination that's allowed is directly relevant to the question of admissibility and there could be no cross-examination, for example, on the credibility of this witness and that sort of thing. But it's all focused directly upon what he did and what he saw and what -- what rights he offered and so on. And it would be a pretty short cross-examination, because I can indicate now that it's not going to be said that this particular witness behaved in -- in an -- in an aggressive or threatening way at all. In fact it's the Defence submission that he's being called precisely because he doesn't know much about it. It's precisely for that reason he's being called and not Mr. Popovic. But Your Honours we agree to him being called, and I invite Your Honour to make a rule about the use to be made of that evidence and whether it's solely related to the question before the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Any response in.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yes. Firstly Prosecution puts on the record its objection to Mr. Morrissey's repeated allegation that we are behaving improperly by -- it's precisely for that reason he's being called and not Mr. Popovic. I've said this two or three times and I don't want to sound like a broken record. In our respectful submission, this -- having reached this stage is not one which should be treated as a voir dire for this reason. A voir dire, as Mr. -- my learned friend has rightly pointed out in the common law system operates quite normally in -- when determining the admissibility of things such as a record of interview or a statement. But it also has the added advantage if it allows the accused himself to take the stand and give evidence on a very limited basis as to the circumstances of the record of interview. And that is not uncommon at all and I know that's not going to happen here. This witness's evidence is very limited. It's limited to the record of interview and the only other point was as to the reputation of the 9th and 10th Brigade in Sarajevo. That's the only thing. Now, I anticipate that the -- that the Defence may well wish to use parts of his evidence at the end of the trial if it goes as to Mr. Halilovic's treatment during Trebevic. So in my submission, in our submission, the evidence should be evidence in the trial and unless the accused himself is going to give evidence as to the nature of the statement, that it's not necessary to treat it as a voir dire.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I'd have to respond.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: You have to be very concise.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I will Your Honour. But the Defence might -- depending on what this witness says the Defence might wish to call evidence, for example from the lawyer. For example, if the Prosecution remain in the their position of declining to call Mr. Popovic but continuing to complain about us pointing that out, if they don't call Mr. Popovic we might want to call him. And we'd be entitled to call him because he's a Prosecution witness who is being hidden from the Court by the Prosecutors.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I do object. I object to this. I object to this. He keeps saying this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Let's not engage in this kind of argument. There's no use at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Prosecution, we submit, ought to call Popovic if they refuse to do so the Defence would want to call him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I believe that you are going to have your case-in-chief. You could call whatever witness you like.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: But, Your Honour, in terms of whether you admit this document or not, the moment is here, and we can't be denied the opportunity to call evidence that's directly relevant to admitting the document if the Prosecutor says they're not prepared to do it. In any event, I took my learned friend to say earlier on that he wasn't concerned and that the Prosecution was prepared to call him. So if that's the true, then they ought to make arrangements to do that, because it's evident that he might be a relevant witness here. And in any event we should hear this witness now. I understand why Your Honour wants me to be brief because we don't want to keep the witness sitting there, but we need to know where we're headed. Your Honour can't be asked to decide this on a narrow basis that the Prosecutor wants and seeks to advance, namely that he'll call the witness who knows nothing about it and not call the witness who knows more about it and then ask Your Honour to decide. So for that reason you've got to consider whether you should do it on a voir dire or not, and I'd submit that you do have to do it on a voir dire because he's one witness who, if the Prosecution won't call him, we might. We might need to call the lawyer. It's also possible that we would want to call Mr. Halilovic on the application. So in those circumstances, depending on what Mr. Okic says, we might have to choose a number of options and therefore it should be dealt with on the voir dire.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I believe we have to make a ruling on this matter. As I said before to the Prosecution, this Bench is governed by the Rules of this Tribunal, and it is not bound by any national rules of evidence, including the common law legal system. So we deliberately not use the special word voir dire, which is for the special purpose of admission of the evidence and directed to the juries in some legal systems. As the Defence said that the Judges here in this court, this case, are professional Judges, so we'll hear the evidence of this witness and they are in the transcript rightly recorded, which forms part of the evidence the Court admitted. It is so decided. Could we have the witness at this stage. Yes, Mr. Morrissey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, we haven't had transcript for the entirety of this discussion, I'm sorry to say. Because it's legal discussion we haven't felt the need for it but I've got a blank screen and I have had that all morning. I just wonder if there could be a brief break before the witness while that's fixed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I see. Let us see how soon that we could fix that screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes, thanks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, we don't want to put you in a disadvantaged position since we are going to hear the witness, so we'll take a break for about ten minutes, and we'll resume at five minutes past ten.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. --- Break taken at 9.54 a.m.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, the technical problems are fixed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Very good. So could we have the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I ask the procedure here. Your Honour's ruling -- the Trial Chamber has just ruled as to the use that could be made of this evidence. Yesterday, you mentioned you'd deal with the evidence in two parts. There's only two parts to this witness's evidence. Do you want to -- do you want me to deal with the 9th and the 10th at the same time or -- while the witness is here rather than break for more argument as to the admissibility which will come at a later point?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Morrissey, what's your response on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, I don't mind --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Your microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I don't mind the witness being add any 9th or 10th questions if that needs to be done. Bear in mind, Your Honour, the restrictions Your Honour placed questions concerning the admissibility of the interview. I take it the Prosecutor will continue to respect those and, yes, I think it's -- it would be acceptable for the 9th and the 10th issues to be dealt with at this stage if that's what the Prosecutor wants to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much for your cooperation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: So we'll do those two things all together. So there is no strict distinguishing between so-called voir dire and the substantive measures. Well, Witness, I'm sorry for having kept you waiting for so long. Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can hear you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Would you please make the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may sit down, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Okic. Some preliminary questions. First, your name is Zlatan Okic, your date of birth is the 19th of October, 1955, you live in Sarajevo, and your occupation is -- you're retired, you're a pensioner, you were a former official of Bosnian State Security. Are all those details correct?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: Just one correction. I'm not retired by profession. My profession is a lawyer who is retired. And everything else is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And you worked in Bosnian State Security, is it correct, from 1979 until your retirement from that position in March 1997?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Were you living in Sarajevo in 1993?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Were you then working for Bosnian State Security?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Were you aware of two particular army units called the 9th and the 10th Brigades in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What was their reputation?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: Not great.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Could I just intervene for a moment. Your Honours, once again this question can't be asked as a double. The reputation of the 9th Brigade is one thing; the reputation of the 10th Brigade is another thing. And the witness has to be asked about those. He can give whatever answers he wants to give but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Re. Maybe you could split your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Not a problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'm going to split the question into, firstly, the 9th, and secondly the 10th. What did you know about the 9th Brigade from living in Sarajevo in 1993?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: Is that the brigade whose commander was Musan Topalovic, Caco? Is that correct? Well, they had the reputation for snatching Serbs in an illegal way, without any legal basis. And also, they used to grab people and take them to dig trenches.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Where were they grabbing people from?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: Mostly in the streets.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Which streets?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: The part of Sarajevo that we tend to call the old town, because that's where the brigade was stationed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Were the people they were taking civilians or military?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: Civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Do you know how often this was happening?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I haven't counted. But I did hear about such cases. I can't tell you how many exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What about a fellow called Ramiz Delalic, called Celo? Do you know --

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: Well, both in the 9th and the 10th Brigades there were 95 per cent of patriots and perhaps only 5 per cent of people who were high-ranking people, but they had a pretty bad reputation. Those commanders surrounded themselves by groups of -- well, I don't know whether I should call them common criminals or semi-criminals, but they were there. So they perpetrated certain crimes such as kidnapping of people or looting flats of Serb citizens who had left Sarajevo and so on. That's what I'd heard at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What's your view of how widely known these activities were at the time based of course on everything you've heard, seen, that's been communicated to you, and your experiences of having lived in Sarajevo through 1993?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. More so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Based on all of those matters, it's just asking the witness to guess and speculate and I object to the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Perhaps you could pursue your question another way, Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I just ask you to clarify the last answer. You said the commanders in the 9th and the 10th surrounded themselves with common criminals, and then you said so they perpetrated certain crimes such as kidnapping of people or looting of flats. Who is the "they" you're referring to? Are you talking about commanders or the people they surrounded themselves with?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: Ramiz Delalic, well I'm not sure about Musan Topalovic, but Ramiz Delalic, as far as I know, had problems with police, and they were the top people within the brigade, and they also selected other people of the same ilk and put them within the staff of the brigade to keep themselves in power.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You referred to crimes such as kidnapping and looting flats of Serb civilians and so on. What's the so on? What other crimes did you hear of committed by members of the 9th and 10th Brigades?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours once again I would ask that the witness be specified when he's talking about member of the 9th Brigade or the 10th Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'm referring to -- his last answer was the 9th and the 10th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, I believe so, that the witness himself answered the 9th and 10th Brigade altogether.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. Well if that's the way the question's put, I don't object to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What's the so on you're referring to, apart from kidnapping and looting of flats of Serb people?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: Mostly that. Perhaps -- yeah, basically those were the two main types of criminal activity that they engaged in. Perhaps there were a couple of other things such as smuggling or things along those lines. But the 9th Brigade was much more involved on the basis of what I'd heard, much more involved in those dealings than the 10th Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, could I just intervene there. I just think it ought to be clarified. The witness give an answer early on when he was asked about the 9th -- the 9th Brigade and the 10th Brigade, and he asked whether the 9th Brigade was Caco's brigade. Now it has to be clarified which one he's talking about here. When he says the 9th Brigade does he mean Caco's brigade or Celo's brigade because that is a matter of importance in the case Your Honours will recall that answer earlier on. I didn't object at the time. The witness is entitled to answer of course but I think that should be clarified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: There's no problem at all with that, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: When you're referring to the 9th and the 10th, you've mentioned Caco and Celo, which one --

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, Caco was the commander of the 9th Brigade and Ramiz Delalic, Celo, was the commander of the 10th Brigade. Afterwards, Celo had been made deputy commander. He was not the commander any longer. But as far as I know, he was still in charge. But I really can't remember when exactly it was that he was demoted.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The kidnapping you referred to a few moments ago, was that the taking of people, civilians, to the trenches or was it another form of kidnapping you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: At that time, I only heard of civilians being taken to dig the trenches. But after the war, I heard and I actually read about people having been killed and having been thrown into a ravine called Kazani, in the vicinity of Sarajevo, but I only read it in the papers afterwards, after there were first accounts published about the war and war crimes. But during the war I only heard about civilians being taken to dig trenches.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Just confining it for the moment to what you heard or told during the war itself, were the things you've just described, the kidnapping, looting, trench digging, things you heard about in the course of your duties or heard about outside of work or a combination?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: Both. And I felt it firsthand. I mean, in my own case I've experienced it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What was your own firsthand experience, Mr. Okic?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: I myself had been kidnapped, and I spent 24 hours digging trenches.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Could you tell the Trial Chamber about that? When was that?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: That was before that so-called -- well, rather, I don't remember the date. It was before that brigade was disarmed and the leadership removed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Was it in 1993?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And whose brigade -- who was the commander of the brigade that kidnapped you?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: Caco.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Where were you kidnapped from?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: From the street.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What were you doing?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: I was going to visit a colleague at his flat. He had invited me to lunch, and -- well. Nothing. I was just surrounded, and there were other civilians there, and I was taken to do the digging.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Whereabouts? In the streets? In where? Was it central Sarajevo or somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: Almost the very centre of town. It is a place where we have a monument to the people who liberated Sarajevo after World War II, and it's called the eternal fire, vjecna vatra, and that's where I was taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: How many -- how many people surrounded you?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: Five or six.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Were they in uniform?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: Yes. Well, what I mean was if you were wearing just a military-looking jacket or fatigue trousers or something, that was considered to be a uniform, because our armed forces were not particularly well-equipped at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: How did you know they were from Caco's brigade?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: Where I was taken to that part of town, there was the commander of the 9th Brigade there.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, you were taken where?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: Close to their command and their headquarters. And then we were taken to dig trenches.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Were you taken to see Caco himself?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: No. No, no, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Were you asked for identification when these people stopped you?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: Yes. And I showed them my official ID but without any success.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Your official ID, was that Ministry of the Interior ID?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Was that the ID that all officials of the Ministry of the Interior carried with them?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What about the other people? How many other people were taken, were kidnapped with you?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: Perhaps a dozen. Ten to 15 thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Were you all captured at the same time in the same spot?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: In the same area, perhaps within a hundred or 200-metre range.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: How were you transported to the headquarters and -- or the area near the headquarters and then to the trenches?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: A van came along, and then we were taken by van, and behind us there was a car with the armed members of the 9th Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And with the five or six who surrounded you that were uniformed, were they armed?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did you have any choice as to whether or not you went with them?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You said you were taken to -- I don't think we got an answer on the transcript to the last question. Just to repeat it, I asked you, did you have any choice as to whether or not you went with them, and I think you said no.

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: No, I had no choice.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did any of the people with you, the dozen or so who were also -- or sorry, the 10 to 15 you referred to, did they -- they likewise have no choice as to whether they went?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: I don't believe so. Had they had any choice, they would have left.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What about the car with the armed members of the 9th Brigade behind you? How many people were in that and what was the function of that car full of armed members of the 9th Brigade?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: There were about three or four of them in the car, and they were there in order to prevent us from fleeing from the van.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Where were you taken to?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: First of all into a courtyard of a house which was close to the headquarters of the brigade and then to dig trenches.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Why did you go to the courtyard of the house close to the headquarters?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: A member of the brigade, I don't know his name now, he explained to us that fighters could not do the digging and we as civilians had to make our contribution to the defence of Sarajevo, and so that was it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And then?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: Well, and then I was taken to the front line, and together with the other two people I was given the task to start digging.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Where were the Serb positions relative to where you were?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: I didn't see them myself, but I heard that they were a couple of hundred metres above us.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Was there any firing?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: No. No one fired at us, not as long as I was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You said there were three of you given the task to start digging. What happened to the -- the other 12 or so people who were also taken from the streets that day?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: The other people left to -- for different places to dig trenches too.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Were you guarded when you were digging trenches?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Were there members of the 9th Brigade there with you when you were digging the trenches?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: Not where we were, further down. We could only run up towards the Serb-held positions or -- or run down the hill to where they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I assume -- I take it that they were armed.

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: You mean members of the 9th Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: How long were you there for?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: Twenty-four hours. The next day at noon I was set free.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Where did you stay that night?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: Near the positions held by the 9th Brigade. There was an abandoned house and that's where we spent the night. We were given dinner, something to eat, and we spent the night there.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You said the next day at noon you were set free. How were you set free?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: A member of the 9th Brigade came along, called my name and said, "You're free to go. Go home now."

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And how did you go home?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: I didn't go home. I went straight to the ministry. I walked.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And how far was that?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: Maybe about a kilometre, kilometre and a half, maybe two, thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Were you wearing civilian clothes while you were at the front line digging trenches?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And the other people --

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: -- Who had been taken with you were they likewise wearing clothes?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: My own clothes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What did you do when you went back to the ministry?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: I told my bosses and my colleagues what had happened to me. That was the only thing could you do at the time, the only choice you had.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What was their response?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: They said, "Tough luck." What else could they have told me? They said, "You should watch yourself next time round."

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What were your feelings or what were you experiencing when you were at the front line digging trenches?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Excuse me. Your Honours, I haven't interrupted up to now because this trench digging that's been featured and the Court's entitled to have some view of what happened there but I -- this really goes to the question of what Mr. Halilovic knew about the reputation of these brigades, and therefore the questions -- while the witness can answer in good faith as to them, the fact is it's now getting to a point of remoteness from relevance to Mr. Halilovic at all. What this particular witness felt about what happened to him or felt when he was at the front line. So I object to it as not being relevant to the proceedings against Halilovic now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, now it's very difficult for us to say that it's relevant or irrelevant and at later stage we have to piece all the evidence together one by one together. So somehow like the crime base evidence in such circumstances and the -- and the -- I believe somebody else will testify about linkage at a later stage. But at this stage, we will allow this evidence to come in.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: As the Court pleases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: You may proceed, Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: May it please the Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Mr. Okic, I was just asking you about your feelings, what you were experiencing when you were at the front line. How did you feel?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: Yes. Well, while I was digging, I was feeling bad about it, bitter about the whole thing. However, later on when I sat down to do some thinking, I was no longer as bitter. At least I'd been given a chance to see what the front line was like. I had a chance to see how soldiers lived at the front line. I realised what a tough time they were having. How difficult it was to dig trenches, to hold on the Defence lines, how difficult the whole thing was. So I stopped feeling bitter and furious with those people. I kept telling myself, well, never mind. At least now you had a chance to see for yourself what it's like.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Apart from the -- the philosophical hindsight on this, when you were actually there you said you were feeling bitter. Did you experience any fear or danger?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: That's now leading and, frankly, Mr. Re, not having got the answer he wanted is now trying again. I object to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The witness answered about his feelings afterwards. I'm just taking him to his feelings about what he was experiencing on the day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, you may directly ask this question. What was his feeling on that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What were you feeling on the day when you were at the front line digging trenches, the Serb positions up the hill and the 9th Brigade down the hill? You're in the middle.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I object to this. It's like somebody performing a card trick here, frankly. The witness has given a direct answer. He said he was feeling bitter. Now, he can be asked why he was feeling bitter or how he was feeling bitter, but that's the answer. It was a direct relevant and responsive answer to the question, and my friend can't really, skilful though it is, is not entitled to do it. So I object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Re, ask a simple question.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'll rephrase it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Mr. Okic, you said you were feeling bad and bitter. What was bad -- what was the badness and the bitterness of your experience on the day of your trench digging?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: Well, it was on account of the way the whole thing happened. It happened in a very bad way, ugly. However, when I thought it over later on, I was resigned to look at it philosophically, and I tried to look on the brighter side of what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Were you given a weapon or any means of defending yourself when you were between the two front-line positions?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Just a moment, just a moment, just a moment. He didn't say he was between the two front line positions. This is now beginning to sound like the Battle of the Somme. Your Honour, he didn't say that at all and I object to this form of cross-examination frankly where assumptions are built into questions that are not agreed to in previous evidence, and as a particular example I object to this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The evidence is the Serbs are up the hill and the 9th Brigade was behind him. If that's not between the two positions I don't know what it is, where it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I think the main progress is to know whether the witness has any means to defend himself. Just stick to that point. I think that's good enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did you have any reasons to defend yourself?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: No. No. We only had our spades and picks.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What did you consider the state of your personal safety to be when you were digging trenches on that day?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: At the outset, there was a bit of fear perhaps that we might get hit by sniper. Two or three hours later, however, we concluded there wouldn't be any fighting on the day, and we managed to even relax a little. We weren't that worried about ourselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You mentioned sniping. Was there any shelling on at that day?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: No. No. Not where I was. Not on that day. No firing, no shelling, no nothing. It is entirely peaceful. The next day, until the moment I was released, it had been very peaceful also.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Was anyone else that you knew in Sarajevo kidnapped like you were and taken to the front line to dig trenches?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: None of the people I knew, but there were quite many people who were taken away like that whom I know of personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Can you -- can you give us a rough figure?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: No. I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Well, I mean is it in single -- two hands, dozens, hundreds, one to five?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know. I don't know. You know, people said all sorts of things. Sometimes people tend to exaggerate. I'm not sure if we're talking about dozens of people or hundreds. I really have no clue. It was a matter much common knowledge that people were being taken to dig trenches, but I don't know how many. I never tried to learn the exact figure.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Moving to the Ministry of the Interior and the work you were doing during the war, I just want you to generally tell the Trial Chamber the structure of the Ministry of the Interior and where you fitted into it. Bosnian state security, I think we've heard evidence of, was part of the Ministry of the Interior. How many departments or sub-departments were in the MUP in 1993?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: I can't say. When I retired, I signed a statement to the effect that I would not be giving away any state secrets. Therefore, I'm more than slightly reluctant to discuss this.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'm not actually asking you at this point or at any other point to give away any state secrets. I'm just asking you about the general structure in the most general terms of the Ministry of the Interior. Like there's civilian police within it. There's security officials. That's all I'm asking you at the moment.

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: Yes, civilian police, state security, crime squad. Those were all part of the Ministry of the Interior, but I'm not sure how exactly they were structured. I'm not familiar with all these details.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: But in any event, the three you've just mentioned, civilian police, state security, and the crime squad, did they all report to the Ministry of the Interior?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And the section you worked in, the state security, was a separate, discrete part of the ministry reporting to the minister, separately to the civilian police; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: Not really a discrete part. All of us who worked with the State Security department were only discrete about our jobs. Everyone at the ministry knew who was with the state security, who was with the crime squad or who was with the police, but we all knew only about our own jobs.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I think there's no dispute here that -- about the powers of civilian police in terms of investigating crimes committed and taken into -- and bringing them -- and -- the investigation of crimes. I want to ask you about state security officials within the Ministry of the Interior. Was there any difference between the powers you as a state security official had and those that the civilian police had in terms of -- I will get to it, Mr. Morrissey, I can see you're about to object.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Hang on a minute. Your Honour, I do object because the Prosecutor here has raised this issue. It's not the witness's fault. He said there's no dispute here about the powers of the civilian police in terms of investigating crimes committed and taken into and bringing the -- them and the investigation of crimes. Now, I don't know whether there's any dispute because I don't know what evidence the Prosecutor's proposing to lead about that at the moment, so when the Prosecutor says there is no dispute, the Defence wants to be clear that we don't know if there's a dispute or not. But in any event, to put that to the witness has no function at all, and my friend should just ask the witness the question he wants to ask him without any preamble about the Defence which we haven't agreed to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Just ask the simple question.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I will. I know there was a very long objection. I was just trying to speed the proceedings up a little bit. I thought there would be no dispute that the police have the powers to arrest and investigate offences. That's all I'm getting at.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Okic, it's true that the police had the powers to arrest and investigate people in 1993, investigate crimes?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: The same as always.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did you have -- were your powers as a Bosnian state security official different to those of the police in terms of arresting and investigating crimes?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: The powers were the same for someone on the beat and the minister of the interior himself. They both had the same powers. They both had the same kind of ID. The difference was that the state security department dealt with political crime, and the crime squad dealt with non-political crime in a manner of speaking. It's only about the type of business they dealt with, but the authority and the powers were shared equally.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And in 1993, what were those powers of arrest and investigation? What could police and security officials do?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: Yes. If there was a crime with a political background, in principle we could arrest the perpetrator. We could initiate an investigation. We could do what police usually do. We could search their flat. We could interview witnesses. We could gather evidence. All the usual steps that are taken by all secret services throughout the world.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did you require a judicial warrant to do any of the things you've just mentioned?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: No. These steps and measures were approved by our own bosses, the minister and the chief of the state security department.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What were your powers of arrest? When could you exercise them, in what circumstances?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: Only if there was sufficient proof that a person had committed a political crime.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What -- what constituted sufficient proof for the purposes of arrest?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
