utterances.text: A report, for example, that a crime was committed, something reliable, trustworthy, a credible source. Material evidence, of course, anything that was gathered, witness statements, information obtained by taking secret measures, that sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: When you say "secret measures," are you talking about things like telephone tapping or surveillance or other forms of covert interception?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: Naturally. All secret services engage in that type of action. So did we.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What powers, if any, did you have to detain people following arrest after you had gathered this information, all the information sufficient to ground an arrest?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: Our powers were enshrined in certain criminal provisions of the Criminal Code and the Law on Criminal Procedure as well as a number of internal rules that we had that had been adopted from the previous system, the old system. The new government probably hadn't had sufficient time to change those.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Was there a length -- a length prescribed in which a person could be detained for questioning or for any other reason?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: As far as I remember, from the pre-war period, up to three months. Under exceptional circumstances, but only under exceptional circumstances, up to six months.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Who -- who was empowered to authorise the detention for that period?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: There was a distinction between nationals and foreigners. For nationals, chief of the state security. In sensitive cases, the minister of the interior. And in case of foreigners, it could only have been authorised by the minister of foreign affairs himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Could a person -- did a person in detention have any right to judicial review of the detention of up to three months?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: Of course. Everyone was entitled to file a complaint, and the prison administration would forward this complaint -- this complaint, as a rule, to the public prosecutor, to the relevant court, or to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What constituted exceptional circumstances?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Will you just permit me -- Excuse me for just a moment, Mr. Okic. Your Honours, frankly this evidence may be capable of assisting the Tribunal and I don't object to it being given, but it has to be made clear whether this evidence is being led as expert evidence, in which case -- and explaining the Rules, generally speaking, in which case the rules ought to be put before the Court at the same time, or if it's just a basis for this witness's actions, in which case they don't need to be put before the Court by the Prosecutor. But if it's a general analysis which it is at the moment, abstract analysis of the law, then this witness may or may not be in a position to give that evidence generally. He is in a position to give, of course, evidence relevant to what he did and I don't object to it. Frankly I can see why this evidence might be helpful but it has to be clarified on what basis it's being led, because in my submission if these provisions to which Mr. Okic is now speaking arise from particular sections of the Criminal Code or indeed from the -- from the procedures to which he's referred, then we ought to have those in front of us in court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I don't think we'll go into the specific rules of the Criminal Code at this stage. I believe this witness is entitled and is capable to answer some questions in this aspect. We'll see how far the questions will go.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. As the Court pleases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: You may proceed, Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have an observation to make. It says that in relation to foreigners only the Minister of Foreign Affairs had the power to order their detention, and I corrected myself to say that it was in fact the minister of the interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You're reading that from the transcript in English?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I see. The correction has been made. I was just asking you about exceptional circumstances. You said someone could be detained, I think, up to three months in exceptional circumstances. Can you just tell the Trial Chamber what constituted exceptional circumstances?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: For example, if we were dealing with a particularly grave crime or a group of people where the investigation entailed a lot more than was usual, if I not mistaken, this was the case with the arrest of Mr. Alija Izetbegovic and the 12 people who were with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The transcript says Mr. Alija Izetbegovic. Can you just have a look at that. Are you referring to Mr. Izetbegovic's arrest in the 1980s or something else?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Was that system still in place in 1993, as of October, November 1993?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: I don't know if it was still in place, but that was the system we used.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Were there rules governing the arrest, interrogation, and detention of suspects in October and November 1993?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: As I have said before, those were rules enshrined in the Criminal Code, the Law on Criminal Procedure, and our internal book of rules.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: In 1993 at the relevant period, who was the chief of state security?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nedzad Ugljen.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: He was your ultimate superior. Were there any levels between you and him or did you report directly to him, without giving away any state secrets, did you report directly to him or to someone else and then to him?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: At the time I had my immediate superior who answered to Mr. Ugljen.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did Mr. Ugljen give you a specific task towards the end of 1993 relevant to these proceedings?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: He appointed me as member of the team that was to interview Mr. Halilovic, who was under investigation by the military security service and state security service at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Was it a joint investigation?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, roughly speaking.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Why were you selected?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: I have no idea. Someone had to be selected.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What were you were told -- what were you told that he was under investigation for?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: Supposed armed uprisings within the 9th and the 10th brigades, and in a way Mr. Halilovic had links to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What were you told these were [microphone not activated]?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: I was told by Mr. -- no. I was told that he had a good relationship with the commanders of the 9th and the 10th Brigade, and when he was replaced that he had asked them to bring pressure to bear upon the then political leadership of the country and asked them to reappoint -- reappoint him as the commander of the BH army.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: When was this supposed armed uprising said to have occurred?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: I can't remember the exact date, but it was of course prior to Mr. Halilovic's arrest. I don't know. I really can't remember exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What were you told or what did you know about this supposed armed uprising?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: I didn't know much about that armed uprising because it was not linked to my usual work at the time, so I only knew from hearsay that apparently the 9th and the 10th Brigade rose up against the military and civilian authorities, but I wasn't paying much attention to that. I was not really interested up until the point when Mr. Ugljen appointed me as a member of the team to talk to Mr. Halilovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Before you were asked -- before Mr. Ugljen asked you to -- reported you to speak Mr. Halilovic, were you involved in an incident in July of 1993 involving the 9th and 10th Brigades?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: I had heard of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Was that the armed uprising that you were asked to speak to Mr. Halilovic about or was it something else?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: I suppose that's what it's about. I suppose that's the event you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What were you told about the pressure that Mr. Halilovic had allegedly tried to get the 9th and the 10th Brigade to bring to bear on the political leadership of the country? What was that about?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: I was told that I should clarify that and clarify his role with regard to his links to Caco and to Celo and would -- he had asked them to -- to do it, to bring pressure to bear upon the then top political and military people and ask for him to be reappointed at the time. And I mean only when I was asked to participate in those talks. I hadn't been briefed a great deal except for what I just said, and afterwards I found out more from Mr. Halilovic himself and Mr. Ugljen told me a few things. But it wasn't much more than what I was told at the very start of the investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And you just said asked for him to be reappointed at the time. Two supplementary questions. Reappointed to what and at what time?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: To be reappointed as commander of the Chief of Staff of the armed forces of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And the time frame?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: I don't quite understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You said he asked -- he -- he was allegedly bringing pressure or getting Caco and Celo to bring pressure upon the top military people and ask for -- asking for him to be reappointed as the commander of the chief of the armed force answer you said at that time. I just want you to clarify which -- at that time. It's at line 52, page 52, line 3 -- line 4 of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: It was before the uprising at any rate. The supposed uprising.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The information you've just given us now, was that what Mr. Ugljen told you?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: Yes. That was the essence of it. I don't remember everything, but apparently through contracts with Caco and Celo he had asked him to exert some pressure more on the political authorities not so much military for him to be reappointed. And that was supposed to be the main subject to be investigated.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: When did Mr. Ugljen give you these instructions and appoint you to interview Mr. Halilovic?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: If I remember correctly, by the beginning of October.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: When you say --

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: The first part of October, thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Were you provided with any information apart from Mr. Ugljen telling you these things? Did you get any documents or dossier or a brief or access to intelligence or surveillance information?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: No. I received no papers. I didn't get a dossier or any report or anything. Mr. Ugljen was telling me things and I was taking them down.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: At what time do you wish to take the break? I'm --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, if you believe that is the right time, we could take the break right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'm entirely in your hands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Maybe we'll take a break and we'll resume at twenty minutes to twelve.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, as for the time arrangement, we'll sit for about an hour, then we'll have a short break, 15 or 20 minutes, and then we'll continue until 1.45 in the afternoon. We hope we can send this witness back home to spend the weekend. So if necessary, there might be a possibility that we have to sit in the afternoon. Yes, Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Before the break, Mr. Okic, you told the Trial Chamber that you didn't receive any papers from Mr. Ugljen, a report or a dossier. He was telling you things and you wrote down notes. Apart from Mr. Ugljen, did anyone else in the process of your interviewing Mr. Halilovic give you any documents or access to any material relevant to your inquiries?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: There is a possibility that I might have heard something in relation to Mr. Halilovic from a colleague or something, but as to the most essential, the most fundamental things and the instructions, not just the information but instructions as well, it was only Mr. Ugljen who issued those.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Before you commenced your interviews with Mr. Halilovic, were you aware or made aware of whether or not his -- he had been under surveillance, such as having his telephone tapped or being followed or any other means of surveillance were employed against him?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: I had not been told, but I assumed that it would have been the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Were you ever given access to anything that suggest -- anything relating to surveillance such as tapes or transcripts or photographs or information relating to covert surveillance?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: No. No. But on the basis of the instructions I received from Mr. Ugljen, I assumed that such covert operations were aimed at Mr. Halilovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What -- what preparations did you undertake before you interviewed Mr. Halilovic? I mean, what did you do to prepare yourself for the task of interviewing him?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: Well, I talked to my colleague from the military security, Mr. Popovic. He was with me up until the end of those talks. First of all, I talked to him to try and find out what they knew, because I was not a part of that investigation from the start.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: How times did you meet Mr. Popovic and where did you meet him before you commenced your interviews with Mr. Halilovic?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: We met at the offices of the state security, and before we started talking, I mean before we started those talks together, there was a meeting at which he briefed me about what they had managed to find out in the course of previous conversations, and then we planned what we would do on that day, what we were supposed to talk about in line with instructions I got from Mr. Ugljen, and he got the instructions from his bosses.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What were your plans as to how you and Mr. Popovic -- firstly, I'll just go back for a moment. Was the plan for you and Mr. Popovic to interview him together?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: By all means.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Mr. Popovic, was he coming from military security?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: Yes. At the time, he was a major.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: His expertise was military security. What was your -- what was the expertise you were bringing to the interviews?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: I was an expert for state security, if I can say that, the civilian side of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did you and Mr. Popovic devise a plan as to how you were to interview Mr. Halilovic and, if so, what was it?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: Before every interview, we would have prepared a list of topics, one or more topics that we were supposed to be talking about on that day, and we -- we would agree on that before the start of the interview. And if it was one topic only and -- well, sometimes we had more than one, and then we thought, okay, we'll do as much as we can.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What these topics in general terms?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: We started out by discussing his career within the armed forces of Yugoslavia and the cooperation with the former military security service of the former Yugoslav People's Army, and then we moved on to other topics such as the armed uprising, the war crime at Grabovica, the fall of Cerska and Konjevic Polje. And -- I can't remember. There was a whole lot we talked about it, many topics.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: How did you decide on these topics?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: For the most part on the basis of the instructions I got from Mr. Ugljen, and Mr. Popovic was getting the instructions from his own superiors.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: How many times did you and Mr. Popovic actually interview Mr. Halilovic?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, the investigation lasted about a month.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And how many times -- how many statements did you take from him?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: On a daily basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Well, how many completed takes did you take from him?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: Perhaps five or six, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: At a moment ago you said on a daily basis, and I think I may have interrupted you. What did you mean by "on a daily basis"? Were you interviewing him on a daily basis?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: Yes, we did interview him on a daily basis, if I remember correctly. Perhaps there was one or two days that we had a break or something, but I really can't remember. Certainly no more than two days, but I think basically we interviewed him every day.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What was your own personal experience in conducting interviews with suspects as of 1993?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I would object to that. It's irrelevant that the witness be asked what he did with Mr. Halilovic, in my submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I believe that the Prosecution is laying the foundation for that. We have to know that, whether this person has some previous experience in interviewing people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I agree. That's true. I withdraw that objection on that basis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: My question is directed to exactly what His Honour the Presiding Trial Judge just said. What was your experience, if any, in interviewing suspects?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: Between 1979 and 1993, in the course of that 14-year period I participated in quite a few investigations. Some were cases that I myself led, and in other cases I was just a member of the team, as was the case with Mr. Halilovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What was the longest interview that you can remember that you conducted before Mr. Halilovic?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: It was when Mr. Alija Izetbegovic was arrested. And one of the people from the group around Mr. Izetbegovic, I was appointed to interview him, and I think the investigation lasted also about -- perhaps not quite a month, but thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What were the standard techniques or procedures which you had used in your interviews up until you interviewed Mr. Halilovic? How did you conduct your interviews?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, that should be clarified between the two situations the witness has described, when he was the leader of the interview and when he was the -- only just a team member.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. I believe in this aspect we could be more specific.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Both.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: When you were a member of the team and when you were leading the team. When I said "you" I meant you plural, not singular. I meant the team of which you were a part?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: When I was on my own, when I was the leader or if it was my case, as it were, I was the chief investigator there, and all the information came to me, and I was the one who determined what needed to be done. But if I was just a member of the team, I had my task which had been assigned to me and I only carried out that particular task.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'm interested at the moment in the techniques or the procedures, what you actually did in the interviews, how you conducted them.

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: Well, when I first started working for the state security, one of the first things that I was told was that a nice-mannered approach was the best approach, and that's what I tried to do throughout my career, to approach people in this way no matter whether they were suspects or simply citizens who were likely to provide us with some useful information. And on the basis of my experience, I realised that that was indeed true, because if you start banging the desk and shouting at someone, that's the best way of ruining everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did you employ this same nice-mannered approach when you interviewed Mr. Halilovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm not going to object to that particular question because it comes to the crunch, but my friend has to stop leading. That's a leading question. Because the Defence is not suggesting anything of that sort with this witness I don't object here, but I don't want any more leading questions to be asked like that, Your Honour. That was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. But on this particular question, I think Mr. Re could continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Mr. Okic.

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: That's the method I used in all cases. That's what I've already said. Never, ever in my entire career have I shouted at anyone or banged the desk or threatened or anything like that, because I did really realise that it was much better to be nice to the person you were interviewing rather than play a tough guy.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'm just asking you about the techniques or methods you employed with Mr. Halilovic. When you say "in all cases," are you including him or were you excluding him from that?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: I think that I was very decent in interviewing Mr. Halilovic, and he can perhaps confirm it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: When you were interviewing him, were you interviewing him as a suspect, or person suspected of committing breaches of civilian or military laws or a combination?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: He was under suspicion with regard to this supposed armed or military uprising. So probably it was about infringing military laws and regulations. But from where I stood, it played no part in it at all. I was facing a man with whom I had to clarify certain issues or, rather, details, and I had been asked to do that. And so it didn't matter to me what sort of law he was supposed to have infringed. I had my task, and I had to carry it out.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: To clarify your earlier evidence, your initial instructions were in relation to a supposed armed uprising. Was it your understanding that that was a breach of civilian or constitutional or military law?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I had not been assigned with the task of looking into the legal, fine points of this but simply to establish the facts and on the basis of what Mr. Halilovic to say. Mr. Popovic and I were not really interested in the legal ins and outs of that. We were only interested in plain facts the way Mr. Halilovic saw them.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Let's go to the interviews now. Where did you interview Mr. Halilovic?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: At the state security offices.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Where are they?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: At the Ministry of the Interior in Sarajevo, in that building. And that was where those offices were at the time as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And how far is that building from the Supreme Command Headquarters in 1993?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: If you mean where Mr. Halilovic was held?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Where he was working.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: No. Don't correct the witness, please. Your Honour, the witness has just made it quite plain what the position is, and my learned friend can't now try to put the Dragon back into the box. He can ask another question, but he can't correct the witness when he gives an unsuitable answer, in my submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, put that question to the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You said where Mr. Halilovic was held. What do you mean by that answer?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: I don't understand, I'm afraid. Could you please clarify in terms of what I meant?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The question I asked you was: How --

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: Where Mr. Halilovic was being held. In detention, you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: No, no, no. I wasn't asking you about detention. I will come to that in a moment. What I'm asking you -- I will come to that issue at some point definitely. I'm asking you at the moment about where his offices were, where his -- where he was based.

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: I have no idea where his office was. I know that at the beginning of the war, maybe in 1993, most of the General Staff had moved out of Sarajevo. They only used some premises in Sarajevo. So I have no idea where his office was, where he was based physically. I assume that it was in a building that was perhaps 200 metres from our own offices as the crow flies near the central prison in Sarajevo. The General Staff used the building for their own needs, and my assumption is that Mr. Halilovic worked there, but I can't say with certainty. I think that's where he used to work before the whole thing happened, and he was also being held in detention in that building.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Just to clarify your last answer, are you -- are you saying in that last answer that you think he was being held in detention or you know that he was being held in detention in that building?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: It's just an assumption. I they the General Staff had offices there. I'm not sure which ones exactly. And I know that whenever we called for him to be brought over, it would only take very little time. So my assumption was that he would be brought from that building. It only took a couple of minutes. I think he was there near the central prison in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I'm slightly confused. What I'm trying to clarify is whether you thought he was in detention or you thought he was being brought from detention or you thought he was being brought from the supreme -- or the General Staff offices.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'm completely confused. I don't understand it and I'm entitled to clarify that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, it doesn't matter whether Mr. Re's confused. The evidence is absolutely crystal clear. He is he not entitled to clarify things for his own benefit. It's -- the questions are for your benefit, the Tribunal. In my submission there is nothing to clarify and the witness has been clear two or three times now. So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, we believe it's also important for the Prosecution to be crystal clear. Yes, Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You understand, I'm trying to work out for the purposes of the evidence for the Trial Chamber whether you thought that he was being held in detention or you thought that he was coming from the General Staff building.

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: I thought he was under some sort of house arrest. He was always escorted by a military police officer. Truth to tell, Major Popovic accompanied him sometimes, the person who worked with me. So I was convinced that he was being held under some sort of house arrest inside that building used by the General Staff. I don't know whether he actually worked there before the whole thing began, but that was where he was being held.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What do you mean by "house arrest"? What meaning does that have to you?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: It means that someone is not free to move about as they please, that they can only move about inside a certain building, that he was not allowed to leave that building un-escorted. He was not free to move about like everyone else, in one word. That was the impression that I had, that Mr. Halilovic was under house arrest, if we can call it that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: All right. Did you have any information as to where he was spending his nights, where he was sleeping?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: My assumption was in that building. That was my assumption.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Let's just go back to where you held the interviews. You said it was in the state security building. Whereabouts in the building?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: No. It was in the Ministry of the Interior part of the building.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I apologise. Yes. Whereabouts -- where did you interview him? Was it in a room, in a cell, what?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: One of the offices. One of the offices.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What sort of office? Just describe its -- general terms, its dimensions.

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: Oh, roughly speaking 4 X 3 or 4 X 4 metres. Maybe 4 X 4, in my estimate.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What furniture was in the room?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: Two tables this size approximately. Mr. Popovic and I sat at that table. There was another lower table with two armchairs, and that was where Mr. Halilovic was seated. There were two filing cabinets for files and documents. There was a low table on which the telephones were kept. There was a carpet. Nothing special.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Was it someone's office?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: I think there was a colleague there who had to move out.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: How far was Mr. Halilovic seated from you and Mr. Popovic? In metres, if you could be approximate.

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: Like the distance between me and your colleague there.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Two, two and a half metres.

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: Thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Was anyone else present in the room when you were interviewing Mr. Halilovic?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: No, not during the interview. When we took the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did people ever come into the room?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: Once or twice perhaps. As soon as they realised their mistake, they would leave the room immediately.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: How did Mr. Halilovic get to your office? I'm sorry, get to the room where the interviews were conducted.

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: First of all, Himzo and I would have a meeting at which we agreed the agenda for that day. Then we would call this other building that was used by the General Staff, and then Mr. Halilovic would come along normally escorted by one military police officer. And then the soldier on duty at reception would inform us that -- that they were on their way, and that Mr. Popovic or myself would bring them up to the room where we interviewed him and then the military police would leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What was Mr. Halilovic wearing?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: Uniform. Uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Was he carrying anything?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: A bag.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What sort of bag?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: An officer's bag for documents, for the sort of thing that every officer needs.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did Mr. Halilovic have a weapon with him?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: Yes. He had a gun. Himzo or I would always remove the gun, place it on top of the filing cabinet behind us, and return it back to him once the interview was over. When it was over, we would return the gun to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What sort of gun was it?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: If I remember correctly, it was a Crvena Zastava Red Flag, 99 millimetres [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: 99 millimetres. Was that nine or 99?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: Red Flag.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Nine or 99?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: [In English] Nine millimetres. Model 99. Red Flag, model 99.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Do you remember whether it was loaded?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It felt quite heavy. I didn't look myself, but since it felt that heavy ...

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: But since it felt that heavy what?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: I assumed it was loaded.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Was this one of these clip-loading pistols, where the clip goes into the --

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, precisely. Yes. I can tell the different kinds of pistols and revolvers.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Have you ever in your 14 previous years of experience interviewed a suspect who had a loaded weapon with him?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: He didn't say, with respect, that it was a loaded weapon.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I didn't say that he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, all right. If we want to play games about it. Your Honour, look, the witness did not state that he looked to see if it was loaded, and to put that question, therefore, in that form is, in my submission, misleading.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: All right. I'll withdraw the word loaded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. To me there is no difference whether the weapon is loaded or not because this witness is not sure whether it's loaded or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Mr. Okic, had you ever in your 14 years leading up to then, state security, interviewed a suspect who had a weapon on them, who was in detention?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: When Mr. Halilovic came for the interviews, did he appear to be -- in what physical state did he appear to be to you?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: Well, in view of the fact that there was a war on, we were all in more or less the same kind of physical state. He looked all right to me, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What can you say about whether he was sick or well by his appearance or anything he said to you?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: Had he said that he was ill, we probably would have put a stop to the interview. It is definitely not the established practice for us to interview people who are ill. That would be pointless exercise. Whenever he said he was tired, we would have a break.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did he appear to you at any stage to be under the influence of drugs or alcohol in any of the interviews?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: I wouldn't say that, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did he appear to you at any stage to be suffering from any form of mental or physical illness?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: That certainly wasn't my impression.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What time did you start the interviews?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: Depends. Sometimes at 10.00, sometimes at 11.00, sometimes at 12.00, that sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What time would you finish?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: We didn't have a fixed time. Whenever we decided that that was it for the day, we would stop. Sometimes it was at 6.00 or 7.00 in the evenings, sometimes at 11.00, 12.00. We didn't really keep track of the time. We wanted to finish our job for the day, if possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You said a moment ago, "Whenever he said he was tired we would have a break." What sort of breaks did you have?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: Short ones.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: How short?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: Ten, 15 minutes, that sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What about meals?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: Right at the outset, we agreed that we would have a break is whenever we all decided that we should have lunch. We had an agreement with Mr. Halilovic to do this on a regular basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Was Mr. Halilovic given lunch?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: Yes. We took lunch together.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Who is "we"?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Popovic, myself, Mr. Halilovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Where did you have lunch?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: The Ministry of the Interior has a canteen, and that's where the food came from.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Are you saying you took him to the canteen or the food was brought to you?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: No. We would make a call and someone would then bring the food.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What sort of food was it?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: I maybe went myself to fetch it once or twice, but usually it would be brought up to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What sort of food was it?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: For those occasions, given the general circumstances, it was nothing much really, but we all shared the same food, potatoes, pasta.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Correction, not pasta, beans. Interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't say it was the same level as the sort of food you're given in a hotel, but we were happy with what we had.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: How long were your lunch breaks generally?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: Depends. About half an hour, 45 minutes, thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What about dinner? Did you give him dinner as well?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: We usually had a late lunch, so normally there was no dinner. Whenever we started at 10.00, 11.00, 12.00, we would normally have lunch at 3.00, 4.00, or 5.00. So Mr. Halilovic never asked for anything extra, and we didn't see it fit to have two meals. Had he so requested, we would have seen to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Was Mr. Halilovic permitted to go to the toilet when he needed to?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course. It goes without saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: How did he go to the toilet?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: It was right there near the office. We would open the door and I would stand at the door or Mr. Popovic would stand at the door. As soon as he was done, we would all return to the room.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What about a telephone? Was he able to use a telephone?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: I think once or twice he actually asked to use the phone. I can't remember specifically. He placed a call to someone, whether it was his son or someone else, but I think he made one or two calls from our office. He may have called the General Staff, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: How do you know who he called?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: He would usually just say, "I need to make a phone call," and then we would just let him use the phone. But it happened once or twice maximum.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did he use the phone in the office in which you were conducting the interviews?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Were you listening to the phone -- the phone conversation when he made the telephone calls?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: How did you and Mr. Popovic ask your questions?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: First we would announce our subject for the day, and then we would try to ask specific questions based on the instructions we'd received from our bosses.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: When -- you say "we." How did you go about your questioning?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: As a matter of principle, Mr. Popovic and I agreed that he would ask questions of a more military nature since I was no expert in the field and he knew more about it than I did. We also agreed that I would ask civilian questions. But there was no strict division, really, and with him the distinction was lost and we would just take turns asking questions trying to get to what was most essential to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: How did you record what he said to you?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: We wrote to down. I had a huge notepad. We took notes. We made notes of what he told us.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: How did those notes -- what did you do with the notes?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: These notes were destroyed long ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The notes, what did you use the notes for?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: There were two purposes. The first was to inform myself, Mr. Ugljen. Secondly, when we drew up statements, the statements were drawn up precisely based on the notes that we had taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What did you write on the notes? Was it the questions and the answers, or the answers, or the questions, or what?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: No, not like this. Not like our transcript here. It was just the gist of what Mr. Halilovic was telling us. We only wanted to know about the crux of the matter. We weren't so much into formal aspects of our interviews.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And how did those notes get into statement form?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: Once we rounded off a particular topic, we called the typist in. The typist would come in. We would start dictating the statement. First one sentence, then we asked Mr. Halilovic whether he agrees for this sentence to be included, and he would say yes or no, then perhaps make corrections, and then we included whatever he said. And the next sentence, and the next sentence, and so on and so forth. The taking of these statements actually took much longer than the interviews themselves. If I remember correctly, it was precisely in those days that we those days that we spent a lot of time in the offices that we actually wrote the statements down.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Was Mr. Halilovic with you for that entire time that you were composing the statements? I'm sorry, what I'm asking you is, did you compose the statements entirely in his presence?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: How often did you make corrections as you were reading the typed line to him?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: I can't say it happened very often, but he would make corrections every now and then. Sometimes he wouldn't like the wording that we used and he would say, "That's not how I said it. I said it like this." Then we would fix it and go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I think you said the -- you said, "Once we rounded off a particular topic, we called the typist in." Did the statements have more than one topic in them?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: Some statements were only about one topic, and some statements actually comprised more different topics.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And at the completion of that topic, what did you do? That is, at the completion of typing up that particular topic, what did you do in the interview process?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: Once the statement was taken and typed up, Mr. Halilovic would go through it. If he was happy, he would initial each of the pages and sign the last page.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What I'm trying to get at at the moment is, did you ever stop the statement before the thing was finished because a topic was finished and then move on to questions and --

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course. Yes. Yes, of course. Well, we tried to round things off nicely and include all the essential issues. It was only then that we would move on to a different topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What -- what was the process at the conclusion of a statement? What happened?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Sefer would initial each page and sign the last page, and would I sign, and Mr. Popovic, too, as well as our typist. We made five copies of each statement, so he had to initial and sign every single page for all the five copies, and then Mr. Popovic and I would sign the statements, the typist would also initial the statements, and that was it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did Mr. Halilovic ever make any corrections to the statements before -- that is, at the end of the process before he signed?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Sometimes there were typos. Sometimes there was no electricity. I think once or twice we had to do it by candlelight. Not typing, just talking. But there were typing errors that were made. Maybe the typist misheard something. Mr. Halilovic, at any rate, did make a number of corrections, whatever he believed was mistyped.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did you or Mr. Popovic or anyone else threaten Mr. Halilovic?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: No. No. I had been given very specific instructions by Mr. Ugljen to be as polite as possible, as fair as possible, to Mr. Halilovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did you or Mr. Popovic or anyone else offer him any inducements?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Just a moment. The witness can -- sorry, just excuse me. Pardon me, Mr. Okic, I'm sorry to interrupt. It has to be made clear whether the witness is being asked whether he offered any inducements, which he can answer, or whether Mr. Popovic did so in his presence, which he can answer, or whether anybody else did so in the presence of Mr. Okic. He can't answer the question that's currently being phrased about anybody else, frankly, unless he can prove he was there and observed that to happen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, he may be -- he may be told. He may have heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honour could be right about that, but that's got to be clarified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, of course. Yes. If Mr. Re would be very glad to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Any inducements, first in your presence; and secondly, did you hear about him being offered any inducements?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: In my presence, nobody offered any inducements. I didn't, and Mr. Popovic didn't, and I had not heard of anyone else doing so. Apart from anything else, either Mr. Popovic or myself, well, we didn't have any powers to do so. We could not offer him any inducement to make a statement we would have liked or something. My task was simply to write down and clarify what Mr. Halilovic had to say and that was the end of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What about promises? Did anyone offer him any promises in your presence or did you hear about him being offered any promises?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: Not in my presence. Nobody did that in my presence, and I had not heard of anyone making any promises to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Was any psychological pressure brought to bear on him in your -- in the interview?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: Well, you know, had I been under this kind of investigation for a month, the way Mr. Halilovic was, I would have probably taken it as a psychological pressure. And I can relate to him possibly feeling that he was being put under pressure. But I can also say that I did all I could, everything within my mind to be fair and kind in the course of that investigation. So obviously I don't think we were putting him under pressure, not intentionally. But if you spend 12 hours or ten hours being interviewed, it may well appear as if you're being put under psychological pressure. I can agree to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Do you know whether your interviews, the interviews you conducted with Mr. Halilovic, were video or audiotaped?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: I don't know, but I suppose. I mean, I can only suppose they might have been, but I can't give you any guarantees there because I've never actually seen any transcripts of any sort, anything that would have been proof of such taping.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Was there a means where taping audio or videoing could have occurred in that room without you having been aware of it?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: Of course, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did Mr. Halilovic ever ask for a lawyer to be present?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Was he entitled under Bosnian law at the time to have the presence of a lawyer if he requested one?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: Of course. Of course he could have asked for a lawyer. And had he asked, I would have gone to see my boss, and I would have said, "Okay, this is the way things are. Mr. Halilovic does not want to talk to us without a lawyer." But as far as I can remember, he never asked. And also, we tried to be as fair as possible, and he tried to be nice as well. And if I may say so, all those interviews, notwithstanding the fact that they were rather exhausting, were characterised by decent behaviour on both sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Who were they exhausting to?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: For all of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What can you say in general terms about Mr. Halilovic's conduct and demeanour during the interviews you conducted with him?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: He was very fair and he cooperated fully, so I have no observations to make in that sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did he ever make any complaints to you about his treatment by you and your colleagues in the interviews?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: What colleagues?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Those -- those taking parts in the -- perhaps I imprecisely used the word "colleagues." You and Mr. Popovic and anyone else who came into the room and assisted in the tying of the statements. Did he complain about Mr. Popovic to you?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: Well, the typists were in no position to insult him in any way. They just did their job. And he did not complain of the way we treated him. I got the impression that he was embittered because of the general way in which he was treated, the position he was in and not our particular attitude, our personal attitude towards him.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You said you got the impression. Did he actually say anything to you or make any complaints to you about -- if I could just finish the question -- did he actually make any complaints to you about his treatment?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: Perhaps --

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry. If we could stop for a moment, please. As I understood what Your Honour said earlier on we're not going to go at this stage into the substance of the interviews. Now, this is asking what Mr. Halilovic said at that time, and in my submission it's traversing into what was said in the interviews.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Well, it's not. It's not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: No. No. Well, I think on this situation we're still on the procedural matters. That is, did he actually make any complaint to you about his treatment, means the whole process of the interview rather than the contents of that statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sorry. If it's -- if it concerns the process of the interview, I've got no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. You may proceed, Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: To be quite clear I'm only talking about the process of the interview and his treatment at that time.

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: Well, he didn't complain of us, of the way we treated him, but he might have dropped a phrase or two on the basis of which I gathered that he was upset about the position he found himself in and not because of our lack of fairness or anything like that, because - let me just reiterate this once again - I think we were totally fair.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did you ever caution him about a right to silence, he didn't have to answer any questions, and anything that he said could be used against him in court proceedings?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Was a caution a standard part of Bosnian investigatory procedure at the time? I mean the issuing of a caution.

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, it was not current practice in the previous system.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I just want you to look at a document. It's dated the 8th of November, 1993. It's Prosecution 65 ter Exhibit number 134, ERN 00997363. Could that please be shown to the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have to inquire what the basis for doing this is at this stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Identification of the document, that's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: If so, I think there is no problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'm not attempting to tender it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I know. I think there will be a problem but, Your Honour, I'll wait and see what's said. THE PROSECUTOR: I'm just asking the witness to identify whether this is an interview that he took, the statement that he took from Mr. Halilovic. It's the basis of why we're here and it doesn't have his signature on it. That's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. On this limited area you could do that.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be MFI 297.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the last page there is a signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Just to be clear, we're looking at a statement dated the 8th of November, 1993, which is headed "Record. Additional statement, official secret, strictly confidential," in Bosnian, of some 12 pages.

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: Could I just see the last page? I mean, I did not do this on my own. We took several statements from Mr. Halilovic, and some of the statements were taken before my time. So I want to see the signature. If it's my signature, obviously I must have taken it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yes. Just look at the first page and identify whether that's the document we're talking about and then if the registrar could please turn it to the last page, which is the 12th page.

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Whose -- there's a signature offer the left over the name Sefer Halilovic. Whose signature is that?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: I suppose Mr. Halilovic's.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: There is one in the middle over the name -- over --

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: It's just initialed by that person. It's not a signature as such. It's our secretary, the typist.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And to the right it says "additional statement taken by," and there are two signatures. Is one of those yours?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: Yes. The first is mine, and the second, I believe, is the signature of Mr. Popovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Now, it would be quicker if I could show him the paper copy and ask him whether Mr. Halilovic's signature is on the bottom of each page otherwise we will have to go through each page and there would probably take a minute for each one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Any objections.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: No. I note that what the witness says, he said he supposes it was Mr. Halilovic's signature. So I don't know what he's going to be asked as to what he sees at the bottom of each page, but I don't mind him being shown the signatures, shown the document in any form the Prosecutor wants to show it to him for the purposes of this process.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'm just going to show you a hard copy of this document.

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: That's a photocopy of one of the statements that I took together with Mr. Popovic. In the course of the investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The statement from Mr. Halilovic?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... signed?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Just a minute. No, I don't object to him answering the question.

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: Yes. It's signed, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Is that Mr. Halilovic's signature on each page?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You've given some evidence about how you took all the statements. Was this particular statement taken in any different manner to the evidence you've given as to the taking of statements from Mr. Halilovic?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Okay. That has been marked for identification. There's only one other matter, and that is the --

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honours. I'm not agreeing to it being marked for identification even at this stage. It's at issue whether it's going to be admitted for use or to be admitted into the evidence at this point. It's a matter for the Court how you proceed with that matter now and its current status.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, marking for identification means nothing. It's just for the benefit of the court deputy and for the Court to find this document in the future.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: It does not have any legal meaning to have a number on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: On that basis I have no objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Thank you. There's just one final matter. Two days ago, Your Honour, the Trial Chamber ruled against the Prosecution on the issue of the second statement on the 12th of November. The Prosecution is considering asking for version of appeal for that particular ruling and we may well appeal if the two -- if the other one is excluded as well. For the purposes of identifying and pre-severing the record, I merely want to show this statement, the second one, and have the witness identify this as the document we referred to the other day and take it no further. If I could do that for the purposes of the record to preserve it for appeal and make no use of it in the proceedings at all. Just so that, if we appeal it at any point, it is clear on the record that the document -- the witness has identified this particular document. That's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Morrissey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: We object to that being done. Your Honour, there's no basis for it being done. It's been excluded from the record, from the trial here. It's got nothing to do with this case. It's not proper to put in for some other collateral proceedings. If -- so long as -- so long as that document's capable of being proved properly for any appeal or any further proceedings there's no need to engage in the current device that's being proposed and I just submit it would be completely irregular for it to be done here. It's got nothing to do with this case in the circumstances. So the Prosecutor's at liberty to pursue whatever remedies they want in terms of certification and ... So there's no basis for it getting a number here in this trial. Your Honours have ruled on it before. It's -- it's over with.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: We're not trying to go behind Your Honour's ruling. It's just for the purpose of the record so that the document is actually identified. I mean we could have tendered it two days ago for the purposes of the hearing or the inquiry into the admissibility. It's just it's not identified on the record at the moment and things get lost. If it ever comes to an appeal in the years to come, things get lost very easily. We only want to mark it for identification. It has no -- no role in the proceedings. The Trial Chamber isn't entitled to use it; it's just that it's there. And we preserve for the purposes of the appeal we preserve the Trial Record as this is the document we asked the Trial Chamber to admit but you ruled against us. That's as far as we take it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: From the point of view of this Bench, we believe that the two documents have different status. The first one we barred from using and, at a meeting, that document at all. It was not used during the whole proceedings. For this document we call the witness, and this may be, there may be a possibility for the admission. I'm not sure at this stage. I couldn't -- I have to make the ruling yet. So that's two different, you know, status of those two documents. We believe that without a number that document does not prevent the Prosecution to ask for certification. As we did in our rulings, we just refer the two documents as November 8th document and November 12th document, which means the statement. So at this stage, this Bench is very reluctant to give a number to that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: May it please Your Honours. I'll finish on this note: There -- I don't want to make use of the other documents, the other interviews, but the witness has said that he participated in a number of signed interviews. I just want him -- I just want the dates of those I views from the witness. The -- it would take a long time if I show each of them to the witness just to say were -- did you take signed statements on these particular days. That's all. I just want the dates on the record, that is all. I'm not attempting to use those, but a lot of evidence has been given as to the ongoing process of taking statements and when they were taken. So I just want the dates from the witness, and if I could just put the dates to him it would be much quicker.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I think that is quite leading.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: It would be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: First of all, you may ask this witness to tell you whether he -- on which date he take a statement or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Do you remember the dates on which you took statements from Mr. Halilovic or which they were signed?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: I can't remember. This was 12 years ago. I can't remember. I could perhaps take a look at the statements themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: If I could be permitted to show the witness. They're not loaded into the system, the actual statements, and say, "Is this the statement which you took," that's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, what's the purpose for that?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Well, it goes to the admissibility of this particular interview, because the challenge is being made on the basis that it was a long, interrogatory process in which there were -- he was subjected, according to the Defence, to come coercion and there were a number of -- the witness has given evidence of having taken a number of statements. In our submission it is relevant to the Trial Chamber's inquiry to know how many signed statements there actually were. The witness clearly can't tell us without going back and looking at the -- the document. That goes right back to Mr. Halilovic's state of mind, the voluntariness, whether he signed the statements, how many statements there were. All I want to do is to -- to say, well are these the -- how many statements did you take? How many were signed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Morrissey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, I object to it. Your Honours, there is a 65 ter list that none of these are on it. Frankly I'm not prepared to cross-examining about them. They've got nothing to do with the case. It's a last -- in my submission if the Prosecutor sought to use this in some probative way, as he now claims he is, as evidence Mr. Halilovic was behaving in a voluntary way, then he should have put them on the list and given someone some notice before this last five minutes. In my submission it's -- the witness has given answers about how many days there were of interviews and -- well, I won't make a speech I oppose that line of questioning and I oppose those things being put to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I'm afraid Mr. Re you cannot do that kind of practice at this stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Could I just summarise -- if I could just summarise. Yourself that you took a number of signed statements but it's been 12 years and you can't remember the dates on which those statements were taken. Over what period were the statements taken and signed? Days, weeks, months?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: The entire investigation, the part that I was involved in lasted roughly a month, so within that period of time I participated in the taking of statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: That's the evidence in chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. My suggestion is that we have a short break.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, that's correct. There's certainly a matter of law I want to raise before I commence to ask questions of the witness and one of the issues is, do I need to ask any questions. So I'd like to raise that matter with the Chamber before cross-examination commences. I can do that at the end of the break and before that period starts however, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: And without the presence of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes, I think so, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. I think we will take a 15-minute break, and we will resume at ten minutes past one, I believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Morrissey, please address the Bench.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, I will. Your Honours, I submit that it's appropriate at this stage to decline to admit that -- that document. It's fair to say the learned Prosecutor did a noble job and went in detail through what the witness could say about the taking of that statement. I objected on a number of occasions, but frankly the Prosecutor was really doing his job and trying to be detailed about what the witness had to say. But what you now know is the Prosecution are finished with this witness and they haven't sought to prove that he was offered a lawyer. It's obvious that he wasn't. He wasn't given the warning that the -- that the evidence might be used against him. There's no suggestion he was told what charges, if any, or that even that the charges were discussed with him by this particular witness. The evidence led at the moment is that there were lengthy, exhausting days where not just the -- not just Mr. Halilovic but the witnesses themselves were exhausted. I think it's fair to say this, Your Honour, I don't want to cross-examine -- I don't want to go into fields that aren't needed and I would submit that, quite frankly, the Prosecutor did all that he could and asked what he could, but the onus is on the Prosecutor here in relation to this document, and I can indicate that if Your Honours were minded to accede to my submission now and rule this document out, I think I've got ten minutes of questions for the witness relating to residual matters, the 9th Brigade. In fact, I think it will be more likely to be five minutes of questions. But otherwise I have to go into the full matter frankly. If Your Honours -- if Your Honour doesn't rule it out at this stage. Now, of course it's -- it's -- it's up to Your Honours whether you -- whether you believe the Prosecutors have reached -- have led evidence that's capable of getting across that threshold, but I think it's fair to say now that despite my objections, I'm full of admiration for the way of the Prosecutor proceeded there and did his best. But really, they haven't sought -- they haven't really tried to jump over the hurdle in the proper way because they have to leave evidence that he was given his rights and that everything was done that should have been done. The onus is upon him. As Your Honours have pointed out, the Celebici judgement makes it clear that whether or not section 42 or Article 42 applied in Bosnian law - that's the standard - it's very hard to admit --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can counsel please slow down for the benefit of the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I've received the usual warning, Your Honours. Now, I can address you further upon it with you I think Your Honour is aware of what -- effectively, what I'm asking at this stage. I would ask Your Honour now to indicate if you were to prepared to do so, that the document should not be admitted into evidence, to spare a lengthy cross-examination. A cross-examination which, quite frankly, would raise issues the Prosecution haven't actually themselves tried to prove. No doubt sensibly, because they know what the witness is going to say. So that's what I raise at this stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Any response, Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Well, it's entirely a matter for the Trial Chamber whether you wish to hear Mr. Morrissey cross-examine the witness. I can't say anything about his application. If the Trial Chamber wishes me to address, I can certainly address based upon the Prosecution evidence as to why we would submit that the statement is capable of admission into evidence, but as to whether or not Mr. Morrissey cross-examines or not is a matter between Mr. Morrissey and the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: You may address us on the second issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: May it please Your Honours. The relevant rule in our submission has to be Rule 95. This, the statement, which is -- I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: MFI 297.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The statement MFI 297 must fall within of itself of its nature of what is in it must fall within the basic primary rule of admission which is 89(C). The Chamber may admit relevant evidence which it deems to have probative value. The subject matter of the relevant statement must be signed by the accused, must be relevant and is probative to these proceedings. Now, I doubt whether the Defence would dispute the relevance and probative value of the statements if accepted into evidence, and to save time I won't go -- unless Your Honours require me to I won't address you as to why we say it's relevant or probative.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, you may continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I can go into detail as to why we say it's relative and probative, but if Your Honours are satisfied it would get to that, test I'll just get to that exclusion, or else I can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I believe you should not address the issue of the probative value and the relevance of the document. We quite understand this document is relevant, and it also has some probative value, but here we haven't come to that stage yet. So let's limit our scope to the first matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I will. So the two -- the two rules of exclusion are of course 89(D) which empowers the Trial Chamber to exclude relevant evidence, that's assuming it's within 89(C), but only if it's probative value is substantially - that's the word - substantially outweighed by the need to ensure a fair trial. In the Prosecution's submission, this -- this -- that isn't the appropriate section under which it would be excluded, if it were. It's a relevant and probative document, and it is highly relevant and highly probative in the Prosecution's submission, but its admission is not -- would not be substantially outweighed by the -- sorry, I put it the other way around. It's in the negative. The words are substantially outweighed by the need to ensure a fair trial. The Prosecution's submission is the accused is of course getting a fair trial and the admission of this document into evidence would not affect his right to a fair trial either by the means of the taking of the statement or the fact that it would be admitted into evidence or the use the Trial Chamber could make of it. The accused has all options available to him. He can call evidence to rebut it, to attack the document. He can -- he has legal advisors. He has the means at his disposal in the Trial Chamber to ensure that there is a fair trial if this document is admitted into evidence, and in our respectful submission, that would not be the correct section to look at. The correct section and it's the primary basis of the application for exclusion is Rule 95, which of course says that no evidence shall be -- it's headed exclusion of certain evidence. "No evidence" -- withdraw that. It's in two parts. There are two parts to the test. "No evidence shall be admissible if obtained by methods which cast substantial" - I underline substantial - "doubt on its reliability" - underline reliability - "or if its admission is antithetical to and" - it's subjunctive - "would seriously damage the integrity of the proceedings." So there's a two-part test that has to be satisfied before it's excluded. The first one is doubt -- substantial doubt on its reliability. In the Prosecution's submission, substantial doubt has not been cast on the reliability of the contents of the statement. If Your Honours look at the statement, it corroborates evidence which other witnesses have given and documents which are in the case as to what happened at Grabovica.
