There is nothing on the face of the document itself which the -- or the things that the accused has said in this signed statement which casts doubt on the reliability, or substantial doubt on the reliability of what is contained therein. Now, that's the hub of the matter. Is it a reliable document? Is what the accused said in 1993 reliable? Is what is there reliable? Is it something which the Trial Chamber could rely upon in convicting or acquitting the accused? If you look at the document, on its face what is there is in the Prosecution's submission reliable and accurate. You've heard from Mr. Okic as to the circumstances of the taking of the statement. Now, no challenge has been made that the accused did not assignment statement. No challenge has been made that what is there is not what the accused said, nor what the accused said in that statement is not reliable. No challenge has been made here through evidence or questions of the witness to suggest that what is in there is not reliable. There is nothing, in my respectful submission, upon which the Trial Chamber could make an assessment that it is not reliable, the contents of the document were not reliable, no matter how long, how many sessions there were, or whether he was in detention or not. It's the accuracy and reliability of the document which must concern the Trial Chamber. And there must be a substantial doubt as to its reliability. The word is substantial. There must and real -- a substantial doubt as to whether what is in it is reliable. And you go back to the methods by which it was obtained. Now, whether or not Mr. Halilovic had a lawyer present or waived his right to have a lawyer present or was cautioned, what you're looking at is, is what he said accurate and reliable? Moving to the second part of the test, which is if it's -- or "if its admission is antithetical to and would seriously damage the integrity of the proceedings." So it has to be both. There has to be substantial doubt on the reliability based on the way it was obtained and, having found that, it would seriously damage the integrity of the proceedings. Now, in my respect full submission, admission into evidence and the use it have by the Trial Chamber cannot seriously damage the integrity of the proceedings. Mr. Halilovic is entitled to all the safeguards in Article 21 of his right to a fair trial and to all the procedural safeguards in the Rules, and the Trial Chamber, we have no doubt, would be extremely careful in assessing the document and the weight that you can give it. The Prosecution submits that it's -- it's a reliable document. It's a contemporaneous document, and it certainly fits within the best evidence rule. It is a statement Mr. Halilovic made within weeks, six weeks or so or - sorry, two months, I'm sorry - of the events which are the subject of the indictment. It's a much better record than you're going to get from his interview with the Prosecution in 2001 or from his book which was published some years later. This is going to be the best record of what the accused himself said about the events in Grabovica, the best contemporaneous record. It would be better in my submission than the accused giving evidence himself because the accused giving evidence himself now will be doing so 13 years later. This is a contemporaneous account which would have to be more reliable because of its contemporaneousness. There are several features I point the Trial Chamber to in weighing up whether or not to admit it into evidence in relation to the circumstances of the taking of the interview. The first is the prevailing circumstances. In determining the methods and whether they cast substantial doubt on the reliability of a document, you have to look at the surrounding circumstances, that it was a war, that Sarajevo was under siege at the time, and that Mr. Halilovic was suspected of involvement in an armed mutiny. There was -- Mr. Okic said there were times when there was no electricity. Mr. Okic himself has given evidence of the behaviour of the brigades who were suspected of -- who Mr. Halilovic was suspected of being involved with according to his -- the chief of security. In fact, kidnapping him and taking him to the -- to the -- to the front lines. So you've got to look at the entirety of the circumstances. And of course they're not perfect and we don't pretend for one moment that they were perfect, and we don't -- the Prosecution doesn't submit that these -- that if that interview was taken by the Prosecutor it would be admissible. It wouldn't be, because that would be under Rule 42, which sets out specific safeguards in relation to charges before this particular Tribunal. Now, what he was interviewed about had nothing to do with what was -- nothing to do with this Tribunal, which -- at that time. It started off with a -- as Mr. Okic said, a general history of Mr. Halilovic in the army and various specific topics, one of which just happens to be, in the Prosecution's submission, Grabovica. The primary purpose was investigating Mr. Halilovic for his supposed participation, I think the word was "in a supposed armed uprising." So he's being investigated for a coup d'etat or a mutiny, not -- not -- not war crimes. So the investigation was for a different purpose all -- altogether. If you look at -- in those circumstances, it is not surprising that Mr. Halilovic was brought in every day and interviewed at some length about a number of different topics, because he was under suspicion of committing serious offences against the state at the time. But the evidence of the way he was treated in relation to the interviews, in particular the one in which we -- which we rely, 297, is that he was brought in by one military police officer, left at reception, brought up to a room and interviewed but given -- but afforded the normal rights - he didn't ask for a lawyer - the normal rights that you would -- one would imagine a person in those circumstances would have. He was given the opportunity to use a telephone and did do so. He was in his uniform. He was allowed the dignity of keeping his rank. He was given lunch, given breaks, and no suggestion or -- or no suggestion has been made that Mr. Okic or Mr. Popovic did anything to coerce him. The highest it gets is there may have been some psychological pressure because the interviews went for a long time, but Mr. Okic explains that, that anyone in those circumstances would be stressed and, of course, that's -- that's quite sure. We don't resile from -- we don't -- not resile. We can't quarrel with that. But one very significant matter, of course, is the weapon. Now, why is Mr. Halilovic carrying a weapon on every occasion? Why has he got a weapon with him which, based on the weight of it, it have may have been loaded. Mr. Okic would be in a position to know because he described the weapon in some detail. That's a very significant feature as to, in our submission, as to the way the Trial Chamber should treat the matter. What is a man, a general, someone with the rank of a general doing coming to an interview carrying a gun with him every day when he's being escorted. He's got the gun with him. When he's brought to the room he's got the gun with him. It's only when he's in the room the gun is put on the top of the cabinet. So in our submission Mr. Halilovic was treated with respect. He answered the questions voluntarily, and importantly you heard from Mr. Okic that not a line was typed up without Mr. Halilovic approving it. Corrections were made, and at the end he signed the document. And at the end of the document it even says as Your Honours -- as you can see, that he had no complaint. It's the last paragraph of the -- "I dictated this statement. It contains everything I said and I accept everything by signing t I have also want to say that the authorised officials during the interview treated me correctly." No complaint has been made that these particular officials in this particular interview, which is what the Trial Chamber is concerned with, did not treat him correctly. Now, if he was treated correctly, the -- notwithstanding that he didn't ask for a lawyer and a lawyer wasn't there, it has the indicia of voluntariness. In the Prosecution's submission, it is prima facie admissible as a probe difficult and relevant document voluntarily made contemporaneously by the accused at the time, and is admissible because it was not obtained by methods which cast substantial doubts upon its reliability noting again that he corrected and went through it line by line before signing it. And its admission into evidence in our submission would seriously damage the integrity of the proceedings. There's one matter my learned colleague reminded me off and that's in relation to the psychological pressure. I was referring earlier to the circumstances of the taking and the times in Sarajevo. The Trial Chamber is also entitled to view the psychological pressures as those pertaining to everyone in the process in Sarajevo at the time. Mr. Halilovic was certainly under some pressure being interviewed, but there was a lot pressure on the inhabitants of Sarajevo at the time during the shelling and the siege, and that's something you should also -- you should also -- you can also consider as not casting doubt on the reliability of the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: There's just one time matter and that is I just draw the Trial Chamber's attention to Mr. Okic's evidence that although the interviews some of them did last a long time, over 12 hours, his evidence was that a lot of time was spent in Mr. Halilovic actually going back through the statement line by line. He said most of the time was spent in the dictating and the correction of the statement, which is another thing which points to its ultimate reliability. Those are my submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, after consultation with my colleagues, this Bench would like to reiterate what we have already said, that is, this Trial Chamber is governed by the Rules of Procedure and Evidence of this Tribunal and is not bound by any national rules of evidence. Any evidence obtained by means contrary to internationally protected human rights is to be excluded in accordance with Rule 95 of the Rules. Where the probative value is outweighed by the means to ensure a fair trial, the evidence is to be excluded pursuant to Rule 89(D) of the Rules. We agree with the Defence. It is for the Prosecutor to prove convincingly and beyond a reasonable doubt that statement was given voluntarily and was not obtained by means of any illegal conduct. We also believe that any accused should have the right to a fair trial. This is an absolute right before any International Criminal Tribunals. The reliability of a piece of evidence is not only on the contents of that document but is also related to the means and the procedures to obtain those documents. Since the right to the fair trial of the accused is an absolute right, so under any circumstances, even in the conflicts of war, those rights should not be derogated at all. We hear the testimony of this witness concerning of the procedure and the ways of conducting the interview and taking the statement, and we hear that the accused was not offered to be assisted by a counsel. No matter whether the accused is well-educated, a lawyer, a judge, or a peasant, this is his inalienable right unless he voluntarily waives this right. We hear the evidence that interview conducted for a month and for every day there was ten to 12 hours for a session. We believe that is too much. The Trial Chamber finds that the statement of the accused was not given in accordance with the Statute and the Rules of Procedure of this Tribunal. Therefore, the statement is excluded from the evidence pursuant to Rule 95 of the Rules. It is so decided.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: As the Court pleases. Your Honours, could I just ask for two minutes to consider whether I have any questions for this witness? I was thinking about that as Your Honour ruled.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And it's desirable that the witness be given a chance to go. If I could just take 60 seconds of the Court's time to think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I think I probably won't ask him questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour. I have one discrete topic that I will ask about and it will be finished by --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Could we have the witness, please. So we might sit a little bit longer without the afternoon sitting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I think it's very encouraging news considering the good weather outside.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Morrissey, your cross-examination, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Okic I only have five minutes and possibly a little more of questioning, and it relates to the question of your knowledge of covert surveillance matters. I understand that there are some areas that you don't want to talk about concerning state secrets and so on. I just want to ask you about some -- the procedures that relate to the putting in place of covert measures. First of all, what procedures needed to be undertaken when a -- a telephone intercept was placed on a particular telephone? In other words, what procedures did an operative who wanted that to be done have to go through?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: Basically to get substantial information which would point out to possible criminal activity against the political background, that is to say indicating that somebody might be engaged or preparing for some sort of activity which would undermine the constitutional system, and that information must be reliable. And then you can start proceedings and, of course, you ask for approval in order to be able to use those measures with regard to a person or a group of people or the entire institution maybe.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. Now, it's those procedures I'm asking you about. For a person at Mr. Halilovic's level of seniority as chief of staff of the armed forces of -- well, perhaps even at an earlier stage, when Mr. Halilovic was the commander of the armed forces in Bosnia, he had the title of Chief of Staff of the Main Staff of that army. But at the time he was the commander, who within the Ministry of the Interior would be the person with the ultimate ability to approve the operative measure of putting a telephone interception device on a telephone associated with Mr. Halilovic?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: First of all, a request had to come from the directorate of the military security and we never used those measures in relation to members of the armed forces without an explicit request, formal request from the military security department. And it was only upon receiving such an official request from them that we would impose those measures on military staff. That's -- that was the practice before the war, and I suppose during the war as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. And apart from getting approval from the -- from somebody in the military security organisation, who within the Ministry of the Interior would have the responsibility under your rules and procedures of approving telephone intercepts on Mr. Halilovic's phone? And I mean within the MUP, within the Ministry of the Interior? Would it have to be the minister or could it be somebody below him?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: I think -- I think formally speaking, it was the chief of state security because he was our national. But I'm convinced that the minister of the interior was informed and, I mean, it was a high-ranking person we are talking about, and I really don't believe that the minister could have been unaware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. And would it be -- in June of -- well, perhaps I should ask you this. In October, November of 1992, who was the chief of state security?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: You mean 1992 or 1993?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: 1992 I mean at this stage, the first year of the war.

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: I think -- I think Mr. Ugljen, the late Mr. Ugljen had already been appointed at that stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. And at that particular time, who was the minister of the interior?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: If I remember correctly, Bakir Alispahic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. Now, moving to June 1993, who at that time was head of state security?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: The same man.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And who was the minister of the interior at that time?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: I suppose Bakir Alispahic but I'm not sure. I think 1992 and 1993, those two men were the leaders in that sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. I understand. I just have to ask you a question. Was it within your knowledge whether either or both of those men were members of the political party, the SDA?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: I have no knowledge of them being members of the SDA, yet I believe they were appointed by the SDA. There was no way to bypass them. They were SDA appointees. But I can't really claim that either of them was a member of the party in a formal sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Very well. Now, I want to turn to questions about the records, if you like, the fruits of telephone tapping when that occurred. When a telephone was tapped was it the practice that an employee of the state security service would handwrite out the transcript of that telephone call?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. They would first listen to the tape and then write down the entire conversation or maybe just the gist of it, depending on what had been agreed with the operative officer or whatever his bosses had told him to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Very well. And did they -- did the typist then submit that report to a member of the state security service for the purpose of review and analysis?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: In principle, the report would be submitted to whoever was in charge of that particular case.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. Was it then the practice of that person who received the -- the -- the handwritten document to put the relevant parts of that document into a report?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: Yes, by all means.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I understand. And was it -- was it required of that SDB operative to put everything that had been contained in the telephone call into their report or just put into their report the parts that seemed to be of significance and importance to them?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: For the most part, I only put what was relevant. People talked about all kinds of thing over the phone. We did not have the resources or the time, for that matter, to monitor everything, especially private conversations of no consequence to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Whereabouts were the records of these telephone calls preserved in the SDB, and I mean both the handwritten documents and also the reports based on those handwritten documents?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: This very much depended on the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. Was there an archive section to which those reports -- to which those transcripts and reports were supposed to be sent?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: There was the archive with the so-called inactive files, files that were closed. But all the copies, all the transcripts were left in the archive. Whenever a file was no longer required by someone, it would be sent to the archive. But there was no separate archive for transcripts, if that's what you mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: No, no. But -- I understand. There was a general archives, but all transcripts and reports based on those transcripts should have been sent to the archives once that file became inactive; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: Yes. Within the framework of each specific file obviously.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. And who is it -- and this archive is under the jurisdiction of the Ministry of the Interior; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: It was at the time. Now that the secret service has been severed from the ministry, I believe it is now on under the purview of the intelligence service or whatever its name happens to be.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I understand. Can you tell us briefly when that severance took place approximately?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: I think in 1996. The -- the agency for investigations and documentation was established.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Thank you. What were the procedures by which a member of the security -- sorry, by which a member of state security could access documents that had been placed in the archives?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Could I -- at this point could I make an inquiry as to whether this has relevance to the proceedings per se or whether the Defence is asking the witness these questions so they could perhaps -- to assist their own lines of inquiry in their preparation?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Well, Mr. Morrissey, I believe that in the cross-examination you could ask any questions so long as they are relevant to this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: So maybe you could be more specific in your questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I can, Your Honour, but the -- the specifics relate to -- the Prosecutor has intended in the past to -- or indicated that they wanted to tender a number of telephone transcripts arising from the MUP, and we want to find out exactly how it is that these transcripts are stored and how it is that these transcripts can be accessed. It's -- they're not this witness's transcripts and I made it quite clear we're not suggested he's connected with them in any way. But that's a great advantage, in a sense, because he can tell us what the procedures are and when other witnesses come along then the Court will have an idea and so, frankly, will the Defence exactly how it is that one gets access to these documents and where they're to be stored and found. So it is directly relevant. We -- we -- we may find ourselves having an admissibility argument on the question -- I'm trying to restrain myself here from making a criticism of him, but we're going to have an admissibility argument, I would think, on some of these transcripts, if I were to put that neutrally. So that's why I'm asking these questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, you may proceed, but do not expand it to some other areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. There won't be any collateral attack. I'll just -- I'll stick to this -- to this -- I've got a list of questions which I think is exhausted in five, perhaps less than five minutes now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. So that the question I think originally was -- I've now forgotten the exact, so -- I'm sorry Mr. Okic, but that's okay. The question is what were the procedures by which a person within the security administration could get access to materials once they'd been archived?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: There's a special form. There was a special form at the time that you had to fill in. You send it up the chain of command and the bosses would have to approve it. First he would be asked what he needed the file for. If it was no direct relation to what he was doing, he would need to prove that it was relevant for something that he was doing at the time. It was only upon that that he would be granted approval.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. I think I've got five questions left now, perhaps six. Very well. Thank you. Now, the question is when a document is proposed to be destroyed, what is the procedure for getting permission to destroy a document, and in particular a telephone transcript?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: Those transcripts were not destroyed. They were archived. There was a special procedure to have a file destroyed. If at some point in a case or in an investigation one concluded that there was no proof of subversive activity, there could be a request to close the case, and it was in such cases that the entire file would be destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: In the case of a file being destroyed, there should be a record of that request to destroy the file being made; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: Needless to say, there's a request by whichever operative is in charge of the case, the request to have the file destroyed with a statement of reasons; why this request was made, to begin with.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay. I just have a question about -- about labelling. Where operative measures were placed against a person, whether it be telephone intercepts or something else, what did the code numbers 02 mean when placed next to that person's name or their code name? In other words, what did it mean that the numbers 02 were placed next to that person's identifying tag?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: I can't say. I'm not sure what you have in mind, 02. We used numbers to mark certain lines of inquiry. Perhaps that's what you have in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes, that is what I have in mind. If a person was marked as 02, did that mean that they were designated as an enemy of the state?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: Internal enemy of the state. That was only for a while, because these numbers changed over time. I can't specifically remember whether that was what it meant in 1993, your code, I mean 02.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. Well, where do we turn to find out what 02 means in the year -- in the years 1992 and 1993? There must have been a -- if you like a book with the codes explained somewhere or some document with the codes explained. Could you -- or could you enlighten us as to that situation?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: It was an internal matter. The relevant people were informed. As of such-and-such a day, 02 ceases to mean internal enemy and takes on a whole new meaning, and then all the branches, units, state security units on the ground would receive appropriate information and the code would then change and be used differently from then on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. If -- it may not be within your knowledge but I'll ask you to comment on this. If a document contained a reference to Sefer Halilovic's code name and it had 02 next to it, at sometime after he was dismissed as commander of the army and made chief of staff, to you looking at that document you would say that the 02 would mean he was classed as an interim enemy and surveilled accordingly; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: No. This number, 02, that's what it said in the heading. It wasn't next to the person's name, the person that these measures were imposed against.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: Maybe those in charge of his case decided to refer to him as 02 as a reference number, but I would need to go back to the original document for that. However, this code, 02, only ever marked a line of inquiry on the face of any of the documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: But the line of inquiry -- yes. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, perhaps if the witness could be then MFI 256, please, the Bosnian version in all cases, please, Your Honour. We're going to show you a particular document here, Mr. Okic. You comment on it if you're able to do so. 256. Sorry. Your Honours, the English version has come up, but might I ask, please, that the B/C/S version be --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I can see here is the letters UB, which means security administration. I suppose it's their reference. And you can see 322 in the upper right corner, and just below that the letters UB. I suppose it's their reference.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Do you see the 0 -- some of that writing is -- I have to tell you is Defence -- is written on by Mr. Dzambasovic, possibly, or other Defence investigators and the -- the words "doc brief 322" would be Defence notations. But it's the 02 below that that I'm interested by. What does that 02 indicate to you?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: 03 on the right-hand side means that the document was produced by department 03.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: But as to 02, I really have not a clue what it means.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: But you can see what I'm talking about? It's in the top right-hand corner there.

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I see the number, but I really have no idea what it's about. I see that the document was produced from department 03.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: And what is department 03? I'm sorry, I'll stop you there for a moment. For reasons of confidentiality, could we just move briefly to the private session here?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. We'll go to the private session, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Finally can I ask you the following questions: When a person was placed under -- under surveillance, did there have to be a formal decision taken to terminate that surveillance or did that surveillance naturally lapse after a period of time?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: These measures could not just lapse. Whoever is in charge of the case must request for measures to be taken or for measures to stop being taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Was it necessary for your organisation to keep records of those involved in surveillance of a particular individual?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: I think in Mr. Halilovic's case all the information we obtained, virtually all the information we obtained, including in document, were submitted or forwarded to the military security administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Very well. But copies would have been reserved at the MUP, at the state security service of that material; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: Only if ordered by the chief of service.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: All right. Do you happen to know whether he issued such an order or whether he handed over everything that he had?

utterances.speaker: ZLATAN OKIC
utterances.text: This is the first time I have set eyes on a document like this, any covert measures being imposed on Mr. Halilovic. But during the investigation itself, I never laid eyes on a document like this. I have no idea whether such documents in fact exist in the security administration or whether all of them were eventually submitted to the military security administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. Well, those are the questions. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Any redirect?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. At this stage are there any other documents to tender? It seems to me -- yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Has that also one been marked for identification?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. It's already admitted, I believe. No? That is --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, that is MFI 256.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: You were, I don't believe it's been admitted into the evidence as yet, but I think this witness has not agreed that he's seen it before. I think in the future the Prosecutors are going to lead some evidence from someone who they -- they say will be able to be an appropriate person for telephone transcripts and at that time we may decide to deal with it in that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, please. Well, Witness, thank you very much for coming to The Hague to give your evidence. After we are adjourned, Madam Usher will show you out of the room. We all wish you a pleasant journey back home. So the hearing for --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, too, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: So the hearing for today is adjourned.
